name: ASP.NET Core
description:
ASP.NET Core is a modern, high-performance, open-source framework for building web applications and APIs. It is cross-platform, running on Windows, Linux, and macOS, and is designed for cloud and container-based deployments. It enables developers to build web apps, RESTful services, and real-time applications using C# and .NET.

Key features include built-in dependency injection, a powerful middleware pipeline, unified MVC and Web API architecture, and support for Razor Pages and Blazor. ASP.NET Core is optimized for cloud hosting and scalable deployments, and benefits from regular updates and strong community support. ASP.NET Core is well adopted by teams within organization and developers can build robust, scalable, and maintainable applications using the latest technologies and best practices.

name: Entity Framework Core
description:
Entity Framework Core is a modern, open-source object-database mapper for .NET. It simplifies data access by allowing developers to work with databases using .NET objects, reducing the need for boilerplate SQL code and improving productivity. EF Core is highly practical for most application scenarios, offering strong integration with modern .NET, support for LINQ queries, migrations, and a wide range of relational databases.

While EF Core is suitable for the majority of use cases, it is not a silver bullet — projects with extremely high performance or complex data access requirements may benefit from alternative solutions. For most applications, however, EF Core provides an efficient, maintainable, and developer-friendly approach to data access.

name: Hibernate
description: Hibernate is a mature and widely adopted object-relational mapping (ORM) framework for Java, designed to simplify database interactions by mapping Java objects to relational database tables. It provides powerful features such as automatic SQL generation, caching, lazy loading, and transaction management, which help reduce boilerplate code and improve productivity. Hibernate also supports complex queries through HQL (Hibernate Query Language) and integrates seamlessly with popular Java frameworks like Spring. Its advantages include reducing development time, promoting maintainable and modular code, and supporting database portability. However, developers should be cautious, as improper configuration or misuse of features like lazy loading can lead to performance issues. Overall, Hibernate is a robust and proven technology, recommended for projects that require efficient and maintainable database interaction in Java applications.

name: OpenTelemetry SDKs
description:
OpenTelemetry SDKs provide language-specific libraries for capturing traces, metrics and logs and exporting them to observability backends. Using the official OpenTelemetry SDKs ensures consistent telemetry signal structure across services, simplifies instrumentation, and enables vendor-neutral export through OTLP.

Adopt OpenTelemetry SDKs for new services and when standardising observability across the platform. Prefer the official SDKs and stable exporters, follow semantic conventions, and centralise configuration (exporter endpoints, resource attributes) via environment variables or a shared configuration library.

Notes: SDKs require careful sampling and resource tagging to avoid high cardinality and cost. When migrating, start with traces or metrics incrementally, validate dashboards and alerts, and ensure backwards compatibility for service-level SLIs.

References: https://opentelemetry.io/

name: React JS
description:
In the crowded landscape of front-end JavaScript frameworks, React.js has proven itself through its declarative programming model, unidirectional data flow, and component-based architecture, which together simplify rendering, promote code reuse, and improve maintainability. Its Virtual DOM diffing enhances performance by minimizing unnecessary DOM operations, and a rich ecosystem of libraries combined with strong community support accelerates development and troubleshooting.

React.js is a mature and well-established framework, widely used across the globe — with surveys consistently ranking it among the top front-end frameworks. Beyond its technical merits, React has emerged as a strong choice in the era of AI-assisted development: its declarative, component-based model is well-suited for code generation tools, and the vast amount of React code in public repositories means LLMs produce high-quality, reliable React code out of the box. This makes it easier to leverage AI pair-programming tools effectively across teams of varying experience levels.

Based on successful adoption across projects of varying sizes, we are moving React.js from Trial to Adopt.

name: Spring Boot
description: Spring Boot enables rapid development while maintaining robustness and enterprise-grade capabilities. Its ecosystem integration with Spring Cloud, Kubernetes, Docker, and observability tools makes it highly suitable for modern distributed architectures. With strong community support and continuous evolution, Spring Boot remains one of the most stable and mature options in the Java ecosystem. While the framework simplifies setup, it can abstract away complexity, which may lead to reduced control over fine-grained configurations. Memory usage can be higher compared to lighter frameworks, and teams should ensure proper understanding of auto-configuration behaviors to avoid hidden performance costs. Spring Boot is recommended for teams building scalable microservices or modular monolithic applications who want a mature ecosystem and strong support for DevOps practices. It should be considered a default choice for Java backend development unless specific performance constraints justify exploring lighter alternatives.

name: Testcontainers
description:
Testcontainers is a library that provides lightweight, throwaway instances of databases, message brokers, web browsers, and other services running in Docker containers for integration testing. Originally developed for Java, Testcontainers now supports multiple languages including Python, Go, .NET, Node.js, and Rust, making it a polyglot solution for integration testing challenges. We're seeing strong adoption of Testcontainers as it addresses a longstanding pain point in integration testing — the gap between local development environments and production infrastructure. The library enables developers to write tests against real services rather than mocks or in-memory alternatives, significantly improving test reliability and confidence. Testcontainers supports a wide range of technologies through official modules (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Kafka, Redis, etc.) and generic container support for custom scenarios. Teams report that while initial setup requires Docker infrastructure, the investment pays off through reduced environment-related test failures and simplified CI/CD pipelines.

We're moving Testcontainers to adopt based on successful implementations across multiple projects in the group — integration tests now run against real PostgreSQL, Kafka, Redis, Toxiproxy, and other services with high reliability and acceptable runtime cost. The main considerations are Docker runtime requirements in CI and slightly longer test execution times than in-memory alternatives, but the trade-off is worth it for any non-trivial integration testing. Teams should ensure their CI environments support Docker and prefer Testcontainers as the default, falling back to mocks only where container start-up cost cannot be accommodated across the suite.

name: Angular Material
description:
Angular Material is a UI component library developed by the Angular team that implements Google’s Material Design principles for Angular applications. It provides a rich set of reusable, accessible, and responsive components such as buttons, dialogs, tables, form controls, and navigation elements. Built with Angular’s component-based architecture, Angular Material ensures seamless integration with Angular’s reactive forms, routing, and theming system. It supports customizable themes, dark mode, and internationalization, making it suitable for enterprise-grade applications. The library emphasizes accessibility (ARIA support) and performance, while offering utilities like CDK (Component Dev Kit) for building custom components. By standardizing on UI patterns from Google Material Design system, Angular Material accelerates development, improves consistency, and reduces design complexity in modern web applications.

Angular Material is already in use across multiple projects in the group for internal agent-facing UI (where customer's do not expect their own design system) where it has proven valuable by providing ease of development and consistent styling across applications developed by disparate teams. Teams using Angular and building applications that do need to conform to specific design system are encouraged to try it.

name: Angular
description: Angular is a comprehensive TypeScript-based framework for building scalable single-page applications with opinionated patterns enforced through components, services, dependency injection, and a powerful CLI. The framework provides integrated solutions for routing, forms, HTTP clients, and testing with strong TypeScript and RxJS integration enabling sophisticated reactive data flows valuable in complex enterprise applications. Angular Material offers production-ready UI components, while recent signals and improved change detection in Angular 16+ address performance concerns. The learning curve around RxJS and framework architecture is steeper than minimalist alternatives, and bundle sizes tend larger though lazy loading and build optimization mitigate production impact. Trial Angular for large-scale enterprise applications where teams value structure, comprehensive tooling, and consistent patterns across multiple teams requiring strong typing guarantees.

name: Cypress
description:
Cypress is a JavaScript-based end-to-end testing framework that runs directly in the browser, offering a fundamentally different architecture from traditional Selenium-based tools. We're seeing increasing interest in Cypress due to its developer-friendly API, automatic waiting mechanisms, and superior debugging capabilities with time-travel snapshots. The framework excels at testing modern single-page applications and provides built-in support for API testing alongside UI tests. However, teams should be aware of its browser limitations—while it supports Chrome, Edge, and Firefox well, Safari support remains limited to paid tiers.

We're moving Cypress to trial as multiple teams have adopted it on greenfield projects and seen real gains in test reliability, debugging speed and developer experience over Selenium-era tools. Projects with existing Selenium investments should still weigh migration effort and team training; teams choosing between Cypress and Playwright should compare cross-browser support and runtime architecture against their app's needs. Despite these considerations, Cypress's architecture addresses many pain points of traditional E2E testing, making it a compelling option for teams struggling with test reliability and maintenance overhead.

name: Quarkus
description:
Quarkus is a Kubernetes-native Java framework that optimises for fast startup, low memory usage, and developer productivity (live reload, unified configuration). It supports GraalVM native images and integrates with Jakarta EE, MicroProfile and popular libraries.

When to use

  • New greenfield microservices, serverless functions or services where startup time and memory matter.

Trade-offs

  • Native-image builds increase CI complexity and time; some libraries need adaptation for native mode.

Recommended action

  • Adopt for new cloud-native Java services; assess migrations carefully and plan native-image builds and testing early. Develop and test with a Kubernetes environment in mind (see IntelliJ Quarkus support and Kubernetes).

name: ApexCharts
description:
ApexCharts is a popular JavaScript charting library known for its simplicity, modern aesthetics, and rich set of features for building interactive visualizations. It has been widely adopted in web applications for rendering dynamic charts with minimal configuration and solid documentation.

However, as of June 2025, ApexCharts has changed its licensing terms to require a paid license for commercial or business use. This shift has significant implications for enterprise projects, especially in environments that prioritize open-source or cost-neutral components.

We place ApexCharts in the Hold ring due to this licensing change. While technically still a capable library, the updated licensing model introduces compliance, cost, and procurement overhead that makes it less attractive for continued or new usage in business contexts. Teams should reconsider its use for new projects and evaluate alternatives with more permissive licenses such as Chart.js, ECharts, or Plotly (open-core).

name: ASP.NET
description: ASP.NET is an older web framework that is no longer actively developed and receives only minimal maintenance updates. Developers should hold off on adopting classic ASP.NET for new projects, as it lacks many modern features, performance improvements, and cross-platform capabilities found in ASP.NET Core. For future-proof, scalable, and maintainable applications, it is recommended to use ASP.NET Core instead.

name: AutoMapper
description:
AutoMapper is a popular library that simplifies object-to-object mapping, reducing boilerplate code when transferring data between models and DTOs. However, as of 2024, AutoMapper has moved to a commercial license for new versions, requiring payment for continued use in many scenarios. Developers should hold off on adopting AutoMapper for new projects unless they are comfortable with the licensing costs.

For most use cases, alternatives like Mapster offer similar functionality with a more permissive license and active development. Consider evaluating these alternatives before committing to AutoMapper.

name: .NET Framework
description: .NET Framework is a legacy platform that is no longer actively developed, receiving only critical maintenance and security updates. Developers should hold off on adopting the old .NET Framework for new projects, as it lacks the performance, cross-platform support, and modern features available in the latest .NET versions. For new development, it is recommended to use modern .NET, which offers better scalability, maintainability, and future-proofing.

name: jQuery
description:
jQuery is a JavaScript library that simplified DOM manipulation, event handling, and AJAX requests with cross-browser compatibility. It was a cornerstone of front-end development for over a decade, but the problems it solved are now handled by the platform itself: standardised DOM APIs, fetch, modern ECMAScript, and component-based frameworks like React, Vue, Angular and Svelte. Carrying jQuery alongside a modern framework adds bundle size, duplicates paradigms, and lets direct DOM mutation fight the framework's reconciliation, leading to subtle bugs and degraded performance. Its plugin ecosystem is also a recurring source of XSS and prototype-pollution advisories, and many plugins are no longer maintained.

Our position is Hold and plan removal: no new code on jQuery, including in legacy screens; teams owning applications that still depend on it should put a concrete migration plan in place—replacing plugins with framework-native components, $.ajax with fetch/axios, and selectors with standard DOM APIs—and treat the remaining usage as technical debt with an owner and a target removal date rather than a permanent state.

name: MediatR
description:
MediatR is a popular open-source .NET library that implements the Mediator pattern for in-process messaging, often used to help enforce Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) and vertical slice architecture. It decouples the request sender (e.g., a controller) from the request handler (the business logic) by routing commands and queries to their respective single handlers, and publishing notifications to multiple handlers. This separation aims to reduce controller "constructor explosion" and enforce the Single Responsibility Principle.

MediatR has recently transitioned from a fully permissive open-source license (MIT) to a dual-license model (Reciprocal Public License 1.5/Commercial).

name: Agent Skills
description:
As AI agents evolve from simple chat interfaces toward autonomous task execution, Context Engineering has become a critical challenge. Agent Skills provide an open standard for modularizing context by packaging instructions, executable scripts and associated resources such as documentation. Agents load skills only when needed based on their descriptions, which reduces token consumption and mitigates context window exhaustion and problems such as agent instruction bloat.

Skills have been adopted very quickly, not only in coding agents but also in personal assistants such as OpenClaw. They're also one reason teams are becoming more cautious about defaulting to MCP, as many use cases can be addressed just as effectively by pointing an agent at a local CLI or script.

As their popularity has grown, the surrounding ecosystem has expanded as well. Plugin marketplaces such as one for Claude, Codex and Cursor are emerging as a way to package, version and share skills, commands, MCP server integrations, and multiple efforts are exploring how to evaluate skill effectiveness. We do, however, caution against unreviewed reuse of third-party skills, as they introduce serious supply chain security risks.

name: Agentic Engineering
description:
Agentic engineering is the discipline of designing software delivery around AI agents that can take meaningful action: exploring code, planning changes, editing files, running checks, reviewing results, and handing work back to humans with traceable evidence. It is not just "AI-assisted coding"; it treats agents as part of the engineering workflow, with clear responsibilities, guardrails, and feedback loops. These workflows are already practical for everyday engineering tasks when kept simple and bounded, as reflected in Anthropic's guidance on building effective agents, OpenAI's practical guide to building agents, and Cursor's agent best practices.

The practice depends heavily on Context Engineering. Agents perform best when they receive curated project knowledge, task boundaries, tool instructions, and fast feedback from tests and linters. Teams adopting agentic engineering should therefore invest in reusable context, well-scoped agent skills, deterministic quality gates, and human review points, so autonomy increases without losing accountability.

name: AI for development
description:
AI for development extends and consolidates AI for code generation from the previous radar. What we tracked a year ago as boilerplate scaffolding and snippet completion has matured into a coherent engineering practice that also covers spec-driven flow, review, testing, and documentation — pulling several adjacent radar entries into a single way of working. The engineer's role is shifting with it: from typing each line toward shaping intent, curating context, and approving outcomes.

We see five modalities, each meaningful on its own and stronger when combined:

  • Spec-driven development — Spec-driven development treats a living spec (plain-language goals, constraints, acceptance criteria) as the source of truth for agents that plan → scaffold → implement → validate through pull requests and checks. Tooling spans IDE/CLI flows like Kiro (requirements → design → tasks), GitHub's Spec Kit (constitution + specify/plan/tasks loop), and Tessl, with similar patterns in BMAD and OpenSpec. Teams typically operate along three maturity levels — spec-first (spec guides one change), spec-anchored (spec persists and evolves), and spec-as-source (humans mostly edit specs; code syncs to them) — keeping human approval gates while encoding non-negotiables in the spec itself.
  • Code generation — In a year, the practical default has moved from inline autocomplete and snippet scaffolding to AI coding assistants that read the repository, plan multi-file changes, run their own checks, and propose ready-to-review patches. Claude Code,OpenAI Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot and Cursor are the common shapes. Treat generated code as a starting point — review it for correctness, security, and licence concerns, and lean on Feedback Loops for Agents so that compilers, linters, and tests catch failures inside the agent's loop rather than in human review.
  • Code review — Building on AI for code review, our practice combines four modalities. IDE assistants flag issues during authoring. Native agent integrations post inline review comments directly on the PR — on GitHub via Claude Code, Codex and GitHub Copilot code review; on on-premise GitLab and Azure DevOps via Claude Code's GitLab CI/CD integration or Codex CLI pipeline jobs (with marketplace extensions on Azure DevOps). Developer-triggered skill-based review has engineers run Claude Code or Codex CLI locally with predefined PR-review Agent Skills on their own merge or pull requests. Alongside these, in-house automated reviewer agents operate against local repository checkouts and post structured findings back to the PR. A useful side-effect we exploit: the same review pass is asked to flag when the change requires a documentation update, keeping docs aligned with code. We deliberately avoid additional third-party SaaS PR bots (CodeRabbit, Greptile, Sourcery and similar) because we are not willing to broaden the set of services that see our source code beyond the AI coding assistants we already vet. None of this replaces SAST/DAST/SCA or secret scanning.
  • Unit test generation — Picking up AI for unit tests generation, AI is reliably good at filling test coverage given a seed: a handful of hand-written tests that establish the patterns and assertion style for the codebase. Teams encode that seed and the surrounding conventions as reusable Agent Skills, so test generation behaves consistently across services instead of reinventing style on every prompt. Developers stay accountable for choosing what to test — AI is a force multiplier on coverage and edge cases, not a substitute for thinking about the test spectrum. Unit tests are the developer-owned slice of testing; everything beyond — integration, Contract testing, end-to-end, performance and exploratory testing with AI assistance — belongs to AI for verification, where the broader QA practice is described.
  • Documentation authoring — AI for documentation authoring drafts user manuals, API references, ADRs, README updates, and inline comments, and performs gap analysis between code and existing docs. Concrete examples: deriving an OpenAPI description and SDK snippets from controllers, drafting an ADR from a sequence of related commits, summarizing release notes from PR titles, and turning a design discussion into a first-pass user-facing guide. Outputs are first drafts, not finished artefacts — humans still own voice, accuracy, and what not to publish.

The compounding effect matters more than any single modality. Spec-driven flows scope what code generation produces; review agents close the gap between intent and implementation; test generation and documentation authoring stay in sync because the same context surfaces both. AI for development sits in the middle of a wider arc — AI for requirements shapes what to build, AI for development builds it, and AI for verification confirms that it works — and it leans on foundations we adopt elsewhere on the radar: Agentic Engineering, Context Engineering, Feedback Loops for Agents, Progressive Context Disclosure, Multi-Agent Workflows, and a Product Context Pack per product.

We are moving this practice to Adopt because teams that combine these modalities deliver faster, with fewer regressions, and onboard newcomers in days rather than weeks — though for junior engineers teams should consciously calibrate how much AI assistance is enabled, so coding fundamentals and a deep understanding of our product architecture still get learned rather than bypassed. The caveats stay: AI-generated code can be confidently wrong; review tools can hide risky changes when humans defer to them; coverage from AI-generated tests can mask shallow assertions; and accumulated AI-authored output without commensurate review accelerates Codebase Cognitive Debt. Teams should keep deterministic quality gates (linters, type checks, unit and integration tests, SAST/SCA, secret scanning) in the agent's loop, treat AI outputs as starting points for expert review, and respect company policy on what code, data, and IP may leave the boundary.

name: AI for requirements
description:
Generative AI is collapsing the early stages of product development — requirements articulation, UI exploration, and prototyping — from a multi-week, multi-role process into hours, sometimes a single working session.

We see three complementary patterns:

  • Articulating requirements: BAs and PMs combine general-purpose LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude) with productivity AI embedded in their tools (Atlassian Rovo, Notion AI) and purpose-built platforms like Aha!, Productboard, Linear, or ScopeMaster — turning raw ideas into well-formed user stories (applying INVEST to story shape and Gherkin for acceptance criteria), running adversarial reviews ("what could go wrong here?"), and synthesizing stakeholder interviews into themes and open questions through research-focused tools like Dovetail or Notably.
  • UI mockups: Designers go from prompt or sketch to interactive draft using AI-native design tools including v0, Figma Make, Galileo AI, and UX Pilot — or Claude Artifacts for throwaway concepts inside a chat. Vision-capable LLMs make screenshot-to-code reliable for digitizing reference screens and hand-drawn ideas.
  • Rapid prototyping: Prompt-to-app builders such as Bolt.new, Lovable, and Replit Agent scaffold full-stack prototypes from a single prompt; agentic IDEs like Cursor, Windsurf, and Claude Code are then used to iterate against the team's own repository when the codebase needs to survive past the prototype.

The compounding effect matters more than any single tool. Stakeholders now react to clickable software during discovery itself, surfacing misunderstandings that previously appeared only in sprint demos.

We are moving this practice to Adopt — teams that build these patterns into their discovery workflow consistently surface misunderstandings earlier and move faster. The caveats are guardrails, not blockers: AI-generated requirements can be confidently wrong, AI-generated UIs trend toward visual homogeneity and miss edge cases, and prototype polish creates false confidence about production readiness — especially in regulated environments. Teams should also respect trademarks, design patents, and source attribution — AI-generated UIs derived from third-party references must be reviewed for IP cleanliness before use in production. Teams should treat outputs as starting points for expert conversation, not finished artifacts.

name: AI for verification
description:
AI for verification extends and consolidates AI for test from requirements from the previous radar and picks up the QA scope that sits beyond developer-owned unit tests — integration, Contract testing, end-to-end, performance, security and exploratory testing. Where AI for development helps engineers build the change, AI for verification helps the team prove it works — and where AI for requirements shapes what to build, this practice closes the loop with continuous, evidence-based confirmation that what shipped matches what was asked for.

We see four complementary patterns, each useful on its own and stronger when combined:

  • Test design from requirements — Building on AI for test from requirements, QA engineers turn user stories, acceptance criteria and design specs into Gherkin scenarios, test charters and risk-prioritised coverage maps using general-purpose LLMs (Claude, ChatGPT) and productivity AI embedded in the tools where requirements already live (Atlassian Rovo). The seed pattern matters: a few hand-written, well-shaped scenarios per product set the style the model imitates everywhere else, which keeps generated coverage aligned with how the team actually writes tests.
  • Test automation generation — Agentic IDEs and CLI agents — Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot — author and refactor Playwright, Cypress, Appium and K6 suites from a scenario or a recorded interaction, including page objects, fixtures and CI wiring. Teams encode their automation conventions (locator strategy, wait policy, data setup) as reusable Agent Skills so generated tests stay consistent across services. Specialised low-code platforms like Mabl and Testim cover the same space for QA roles that prefer a UI-driven loop over an IDE.
  • Test result triage and flake analysis — Modern test reporting platforms (Report Portal, Allure Report) cluster failures by signature and use ML-based auto-analysis to suggest whether a red test is a known defect, a product bug or an automation issue — turning a wall of red runs into a short, ranked list of things actually worth a human's attention. Layered on top of our Test Reporting and Test management tools tooling, this is the pattern where AI moves the needle most for testers today: less time tagging flakes, more time testing.
  • Security and performance verification — AI assists triage of findings from SonarQube, ZAP (OWASP ZAP) and SCA tooling, drafts Factory acceptance testing checklists from threat models, and helps interpret K6 performance runs against historical baselines so regressions are flagged in language a release manager can act on. None of this replaces the underlying scanners or load tools — it makes their output digestible at the cadence releases actually move.

The compounding effect matters more than any single pattern. Generated scenarios feed generated automation; consistent automation produces clean run history; clean history makes triage AI's signal sharp; sharp signal frees QA effort to invest in exploratory and security testing where AI is still a junior partner. AI for verification leans on the same foundations as the rest of the AI practice on this radar: Agent Skills, Feedback Loops for Agents, Context Engineering, and a Product Context Pack per product so the agent understands the system under test, not just the test framework.

We are placing this practice in Adopt because teams that combine these patterns get broader test coverage with less manual effort, and move faster from a failed run to a fixed defect. The caveats stay: AI-generated tests can pass for the wrong reasons, auto-triage can hide real regressions, and AI-authored test code without proper review adds to Codebase Cognitive Debt in the test suite itself. Treat AI as a force multiplier for the testers we have, keep deterministic gates (smoke suites, contract checks, security scans) in the pipeline regardless of what the agent thinks, and respect company policy on what code and data may leave the boundary.

name: API First
description:
API First is an approach to software design where APIs are treated as first-class citizens and defined before any implementation begins. Instead of building an application and then exposing APIs as an afterthought, teams start by designing the API contract—often using specifications like OpenAPI or AsyncAPI—to ensure clarity, consistency, and interoperability.

This approach is currently used succesfully by many teams in our group, and we encourage others to try it in their future projects. Designing APIs first promotes consumer-driven design, enabling parallel development across teams, better alignment with business requirements, and seamless integration within distributed or microservices architectures. It also supports automated workflows such as mock servers, Contract testing, and code generation, helping reduce errors and accelerate delivery. By prioritizing APIs early, organizations create more maintainable, scalable, and reusable services, which is critical for modern ecosystems where APIs are the backbone of digital platforms.

API First is also becoming a critical foundation for working effectively with AI. A well-defined OpenAPI or AsyncAPI specification gives coding agents a precise, machine-readable contract they can reason about, generate clients and servers from, and validate their output against. The same contract powers MCP servers and tool definitions exposed to agents, ensures AI-generated implementations stay aligned with the agreed interface, and integrates naturally with Feedback Loops for Agents and Contract testing so that drift is caught immediately. In an era where AI accelerates code production, the API contract becomes the source of truth that keeps humans, agents, and services speaking the same language.

name: Automated Dependency Updates
description:
Automated Dependency Updates is a key technique in modern software development. It involves tools that automatically detect outdated dependencies, create automated pull requests (PRs) for updates, and often incorporate security vulnerability scanning to reduce maintenance burden and mitigate supply chain risks.

With the widespread usage of AI tools, dependencies update frequently, creating a constant need for timely patches to maintain security.

Dependabot (GitHub) Native GitHub tool that automatically generates version and security update PRs. Supports 20+ package managers. Free for public repositories and included in GitHub plans for private ones.

Renovate (Mend Renovate) Highly configurable open-source tool (AGPL) supporting over 90 package managers and multiple platforms (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps). Excellent monorepo and customization support. Free self-hosted/on-premise deployment (CLI/Docker) under AGPL, ideal for internal or air-gapped setups; enterprise options for advanced features.

Dependabot is a reliable baseline solution for GitHub-based teams, for on premise self-hosted installations go for Renovate.

name: Clean Architecture
description:
Clean Architecture is a software design approach that emphasizes separation of concerns, independence from frameworks, and testability by organizing code into concentric layers with strict dependency rules. The core principle is that dependencies point inward toward business logic, ensuring the domain layer remains independent of external concerns like UI, databases, or frameworks. Various implementations exist including layered architecture, hexagonal architecture, and ports and adapters patterns, all sharing the goal of decoupling business rules from infrastructure details.

Clean Architecture provides significant benefits including improved testability through isolated business logic, flexibility to swap frameworks or databases without impacting core functionality, and clearer code organization that aids long-term maintainability. Teams adopting these patterns consistently report better separation between domain logic and technical implementation, making systems easier to understand, modify, and extend. We're placing Clean Architecture in adopt based on its proven effectiveness across projects of varying sizes and complexity. Teams should apply these principles pragmatically, understanding that the investment in proper layering and dependency management pays dividends through reduced coupling and enhanced maintainability. For new projects and major refactoring efforts, particularly with frameworks like Spring Boot, Clean Architecture provides a solid foundation for building sustainable, evolvable systems.

Clean Architecture takes on renewed importance as AI accelerates code production. Agents work best against codebases with clear seams; without them, AI-generated code drifts into layer violations that erode the team's shared mental model — exactly the Codebase Cognitive Debt we want to avoid. Clear layering also makes Context Engineering tractable (an agent can be fed a focused slice rather than the whole repository) and lets architectural rules run as part of Feedback Loops for Agents — see Architecture as Code for the enforcement story.

name: Context Engineering
description:
Context engineering is the practice of deliberately shaping the information an AI agent sees while it works: instructions, examples, repository knowledge, tool descriptions, feedback signals, and task-specific constraints. It moves teams beyond one-off prompt writing toward a repeatable engineering discipline for keeping the agent's context relevant, compact, and grounded in the actual system. Context quality is now one of the main factors that determines whether agentic workflows are reliable or noisy; useful references include OpenAI's guide to prompt engineering and Cursor's docs on rules.

This is a foundation for Agentic Engineering. If agentic workflows are expected to plan, edit, test, review, or coordinate work across tools, the quality of their context becomes part of the delivery system. Good context engineering uses patterns such as progressive context disclosure, agent skills, context packs, and feedback loops so agents receive enough information to act well without drowning in irrelevant instructions.

name: Continuous delivery
description:
Continuous Delivery (CD) automates the preparation and deployment of software, enabling each version to be potentially releasable at any time. This practice relies on automated pipelines that validate, package, and deploy changes consistently. It takes after Continuous integration.

Its implementation ensures a traceable, automated software lifecycle aligned with principles of observability and immutable deployments. It also increases delivery speed, operational stability, and business responsiveness. By reducing manual errors and facilitating a predictable deployment flow, Continuous Delivery (CD) becomes a key pillar for multi-organization ecosystems or environments with multiple production stages. It further enhances collaboration between development and operations [DevOps] (../PP/devops.md) teams.

name: Continuous integration
description:
Continuous Integration (CI) is a DevOps practice that automates code compilation, testing, and validation every time a developer makes changes to the repository. It ensures that the software remains always integrable and functional.

Adopting Continuous Integration (CI) allows teams to detect issues early, improve code quality, and reduce integration time across teams. Continuous Integration promotes discipline in collaborative development and sets the foundation for more advanced practices such as Continuous delivery and test automation. In complex or distributed enterprise environments, Continuous Integration (CI) adoption is a need and results in greater traceability, source code consistency, and version control.

name: DevOps
description:
What

  • DevOps is the combination of cultural practices, automation, and measurable operational processes (CI/CD, Infrastructure as Code, automated testing, observability, and continuous delivery) that enable fast, safe, repeatable delivery of software.

Why now

  • Business demands faster delivery and reliable operations. DevOps reduces lead time, increases deployment frequency and improves recovery time with small, testable changes and continuous feedback loops.

When to adopt

  • Adopt when you need faster iteration, better alignment between teams, predictable releases, and improved reliability. Start with CI, trunk-based development, automated tests, and progressive delivery; grow toward IaC, observability and SRE practices.

Considerations

  • Culture change is the hardest part: invest in cross-functional teams, shared SLIs/SLOs, and blameless postmortems.
  • Prioritize automation and incremental rollout; avoid big-bang transformations.
  • Secure by design: integrate security checks early (shift-left).

Key practices

  • Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery (CI/CD)
  • Infrastructure as Code (Terraform, CloudFormation)
  • Observability (metrics, logs, traces)
  • Trunk-based development and feature flags
  • Blameless postmortems and SLO-driven operations

Further reading

  • https://about.google/intl/en/products/sre/
  • https://martinfowler.com/bliki/ContinuousDelivery.html
  • https://12factor.net

name: Feedback Loops for Agents
description:
Coding agents become dramatically more useful — and far less expensive for their human reviewers — when the same deterministic quality gates we already trust (compilers, linters, type checkers, structural tests, unit and integration suites) are wired directly into the agent's loop. Instead of waiting for a human to notice a broken build or a failing test in review, the agent observes the failure itself and self-corrects, producing cleaner output before any commit lands. This is the core idea behind ThoughtWorks' feedback sensors for coding agents: treat established checks as a backpressure mechanism that the agent can read.

In practice, teams wire this up in a few different shapes — a reviewer agent that runs checks and triggers corrections, a long-running companion process the agent can query, or a thin CLI the agent invokes between edits. Coding agents also lower the cost of authoring custom linters and structural assertions, so the catalogue of feedback the agent receives can grow with the team's conventions. Whenever possible, these checks should run during the coding session, not as a post-commit afterthought. The further the failure signal is from the agent's working context, the less of it actually closes the loop.

name: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code expresses compute, network, storage, and platform configuration as versioned, reviewable code. Declarative definitions produce reproducible environments, reduce configuration drift, and make changes auditable. Provisioning tools such as Terraform manage cloud and on-prem resources, while Ansible and image builders like Packer configure operating systems and middleware. Kubernetes manifests are packaged with Helm or shaped with Kustomize and reconciled by GitOps controllers such as Argo CD or Flux. Guardrails arise naturally from the workflow: pull requests, automated plans, policy checks, and continuous reconciliation highlight unintended changes before they reach production. Secrets remain outside version control in a vault or KMS, and remote state backends provide locking and encryption. The result is faster recovery through re-creation, consistent environments across data centers, and a clear change history that satisfies operational and compliance needs.

name: Microfrontends
description: Microfrontends extend Microservices principles to frontend development by decomposing user interfaces into independently deployable, team-owned modules that compose at runtime or build time. Each microfrontend encapsulates a business domain with its own technology stack, deployment pipeline, and lifecycle, integrating through framework-agnostic patterns like web components, module federation, iframe isolation, or server-side composition. Common integration approaches include Webpack Module Federation for runtime sharing, single-spa for framework orchestration, or edge-side composition with CDN routing. The architecture enables autonomous team velocity with independent deployments, technology diversity for evolving frameworks, and incremental migration from monolithic frontends. Challenges include managing shared dependencies to prevent bundle duplication, coordinating cross-cutting concerns like authentication and styling, maintaining consistent UX across boundaries, and ensuring performance with multiple framework runtimes. Adopt microfrontends for large-scale applications with multiple teams requiring independent delivery cadences and clear domain boundaries, establishing governance for shared libraries, design systems, and communication protocols between modules.

name: Progressive Context Disclosure
description:
Progressive context disclosure is a Context Engineering technique that flips the usual instinct of front-loading every rule and reference an agent might ever need. Instead, the agent starts with a lightweight index of what's available — domains, tools, skills, documents — and only pulls the detailed material into its context window once it has seen the user's prompt and decided what is actually relevant. The result is a much higher signal-to-noise ratio per token spent.

The pattern shows up in two places we already work with. In retrieval pipelines, the agent first decides which corner of the knowledge base matches the question and then retrieves the specific chunks it needs. In coding agents, it is how Agent Skills are loaded: the agent inspects skill descriptions, picks the few that fit the task, and only then reads their full instructions. This avoids the failure mode of an ever-growing monolithic prompt stuffed with conditional "do this except when…" rules, which models attend to less reliably as the context grows. Disclosing context progressively keeps the working window lean and helps the agent stay focused on the task at hand.

name: Structured Logging
description: Structured logging provides significant benefits by capturing log data in a consistent, machine-readable format, such as JSON. This approach enables powerful analytics and querying capabilities, making it easier to identify patterns, troubleshoot issues, and monitor application health. Structured logs are especially practical during load tests and high-traffic scenarios, as they allow for efficient aggregation and analysis of large volumes of data. By adopting structured logging, teams can improve observability, streamline debugging, and gain deeper insights into system behavior.

name: Agile Development
description:
Agile development is an iterative and people-centric approach to software delivery, governed by the Agile Manifesto’s (https://agilemanifesto.org/) four values and twelve principles. It prioritizes Individuals and interactions over processes and tools, Working software over comprehensive documentation, Customer collaboration over contract negotiation, and Responding to change over following a plan.

Work is organized into short, fixed-length cycles (Sprints or iterations), enabling frequent feedback loops, early validation, and continuous delivery of incremental value. Requirements are managed dynamically through a prioritized backlog, allowing teams to continuously refine scope based on business value, customer feedback, and emerging insights.

Agile emphasizes not only delivery cadence, but also strong engineering practices such as continuous integration, automated testing, and regular refactoring to sustain long-term quality and adaptability. Continuous improvement is a core aspect, with teams regularly inspecting and adapting their ways of working through feedback mechanisms such as retrospectives.

While Agile benefits are well established, its successful adoption depends on both organizational and team maturity. It requires active customer involvement, empowered cross-functional teams, and a shared understanding of ownership and accountability. Simply adopting Agile ceremonies without embracing its underlying principles and engineering discipline can lead to scope creep, technical debt, reduced transparency, and lack of predictability.

A new project should therefore selectively pilot Agile practices (such as daily stand-ups, short iterations, and continuous integration) to validate the team’s ability to operate within the Agile mindset before scaling its adoption.

name: Architecture as Code
description:
Treating architecture as code means encoding the qualities we expect from a system — modularity, layering, dependency direction, performance budgets, security constraints — as executable checks that run in the same pipelines as our builds and tests. The idea draws on the architectural fitness function concept popularised by Building Evolutionary Architectures: an objective, automated assessment of one or more architectural characteristics, expressed through unit tests, structural rules, metrics or runtime monitors. Tools like ArchUnit, Spectral and module-boundary checks in frameworks such as Spring Modulith make it practical to express these rules alongside the code they govern.

Encoding architecture this way pays off most where humans cannot keep up with the rate of change. As AI-assisted delivery accelerates output and contributes to Codebase Cognitive Debt, executable architectural rules become a continuous feedback channel that prevents drift before review. Combined with Feedback Loops for Agents, they let coding agents self-correct against the team's intended design instead of replicating whatever pattern they happen to find nearby.

name: CQRS
description: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) separates read and write operations into distinct models where commands modify state through domain logic enforcing business rules while queries retrieve data optimized for specific use cases without side effects. This enables independent scaling and evolution of read/write paths, particularly valuable in high-throughput systems with asymmetric patterns. CQRS pairs naturally with event sourcing for audit trails and temporal queries, allowing varied projections of the same data—customer views, fulfillment operations, analytics, search—each optimized for access patterns and consistency requirements. The pattern introduces complexity through synchronization mechanisms, eventual consistency reasoning, projection rebuilds, and schema evolution across models, often via Event-driven architecture or message queues. Trial CQRS in bounded contexts with high read/write asymmetry, specialized query needs, complex domain logic, or audit requirements, avoiding simple CRUD operations or scenarios requiring strict immediate consistency.

name: Event-driven architecture
description:
Event-driven architecture is a software design pattern where components react to and communicate through events—changes in system state—rather than direct synchronous requests. Producers emit events without needing to know who will consume them, and consumers respond asynchronously, with only the event format acting as a shared contract. The result is a loosely coupled, scalable, and resilient system that can react to information in real time.

Because dependencies are reduced to the event schema, services can be updated, replaced, or scaled independently based on their event load, and a temporary outage of a consumer is absorbed by the broker until it recovers—making the system naturally fault-tolerant and a strong fit for use cases like fraud detection, inventory management, and personalized user experiences. In practice the pattern also pairs exceptionally well with AI-assisted development: each microservice stays small, focused, and easy to integrate, which lets AI agents lead day-to-day implementation while the system design engineer absorbs the architectural complexity—enabling junior developers and AI agents to deliver complex systems together. Evolving the design within the same pattern is equally straightforward; swapping a consumer, adding a new reaction to an existing event, or extending a flow rarely ripples beyond the touched component, so iteration stays cheap as the system grows.

name: Factory acceptance testing
description:
Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT), is a pre-shipment process where deliverables are tested by vendor to verify it meets all specifications, design criteria, and functional requirements before being released to the market. When a product team delivers a packaged software for on-premises deployment, factory acceptance testing (FAT) ensures that product deliverables operate correctly in a realistic, production-like environment. FAT typically encompasses multiple testing dimensions — functional verification, performance benchmarking, and basic security validation — depending on product type and risk profile. The practice increasingly relies on automation frameworks to execute regression and performance suites and can vary in scope from module-level validation of subsystems to full product-level end‑to‑end acceptance.

Adoption will help teams reduce defect escape rate, post-delivery incidents, ensure environment reproducibility, and shorten customer acceptance cycles. The main challenge remains in balancing realistic test environments with efficient automation.

name: Feedback Flywheel
description:
Most teams adopting coding agents settle into some variant of a spec → plan → implement workflow. The feedback flywheel adds an explicit fourth step that closes the loop on the agent harness itself: after a session, capture what worked and what didn't, then improve the inputs to the next session. It is essentially a retrospective applied to the way the team collaborates with the agent, and the gains compound as the harness gets sharper over time.

Concretely, the flywheel turns observed failures into changes to the things that drive future runs — the project's curated instructions, the Feedback Loops for Agents, the prompt templates, the small skills the team relies on. A human is still on the loop here, deciding which signals are noise and which are systemic. The technique is particularly worth running every time a new model is rolled in: prompts and rules tuned for last quarter's model often add friction with the next one, and the flywheel is the cheapest way to find out which parts of the harness are still earning their place.

name: Microservices
description: Microservices is an architectural style that organizes software into small, independently deployable services with clear bounded contexts. Each service owns its data and exposes contracts through APIs or events, enabling teams to iterate and scale components separately. Communication favors asynchronous messaging for decoupling and resilience, with synchronous calls reserved for request/response needs and protected by timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers. Operational autonomy improves when services publish uniform health endpoints, metrics, and traces, allowing platform tooling to automate rollouts and failure handling. The approach introduces new responsibilities—contract versioning, schema evolution, cross-service debugging, and eventual consistency—mitigated by patterns such as outbox/CDC, sagas for multi-step flows, and schema registries. Microservices fit best where domain boundaries are strong and deployment velocity matters more than in-process calls.

name: OSS license checks
description:
With frequent changes of licenses in open-source projects and LLM tools producing snippets they learned from open codebases, open-source license compliance is becoming a necessary part of continuous delivery pipelines. Modern tools like Snyk, FOSSA, ScanCode can detect non-compliant or risky licenses (GPL, AGPL, SSPL) before release. Integrating automated license verification into CI/CD protects us from downstream legal exposure and helps procurement vet third-party dependencies at scale.

Teams should explorie policy-as-code enforcement to block merges or releases when high-risk licenses appear. The goal is to move license validation from manual review to a repeatable, auditable pipeline control, embedded in the same way we treat static analysis or vulnerability scans today. Over time this practice should become mature part of our secure software supply-chain posture — but adoption cost and scanning noise remain real challenges.

name: Contract testing
description:
Traditional integration tests spin up full environments and exercise multiple services simultaneously, which introduces heavy setup costs, long execution times, and high flakiness where a small environment or data issue can break dozens of tests.

In contrast, contract tests focus on the API agreements between services: consumers and/or providers define expectations, and each provider verifies that it still satisfies those expectations. Because these tests run in isolation with lightweight mocks or stubs, they detect compatibility issues early in CI pipelines without requiring full system orchestration.

Consumer-driven contracts and tools such as Pact let downstream consumers define assertions that are executed in provider flows. In addition, provider-driven contract flows validate backward compatibility with API conformance tests and contract change validation. Modern setups integrate contract tests into CI to flag breaking API changes early and publish verified contracts to registries like Pact Broker.

Teams should treat contract tests as executable documentation between squads and as input to release automation. The challenge is governance: versioning, schema evolution, and when to allow breaking changes.

name: Domain Driven Design
description:
Domain-Driven Design (DDD) is an architectural philosophy and set of practices centered around connecting the implementation with an evolving model of the core business domain. It involves deep collaboration with domain experts to distill a Ubiquitous Language—a shared vocabulary used by both developers and business users in the code and documentation. Key patterns include Aggregates, Entities, and Value Objects, all operating within explicitly defined Bounded Contexts to manage complexity and ensure the software accurately reflects the business's reality.

Our experience on the Digital Core programme has been positive: aligning teams around a Ubiquitous Language and explicit Bounded Contexts produced clearer service boundaries, less integration friction, and modules that are easier to evolve as business requirements change. The investment in modelling sessions paid back in fewer rework cycles and more stable APIs. DDD still requires deep domain expertise, developer discipline, and can be over-engineering for simple CRUD applications—so teams should keep researching the approach before committing—but for complex, long-lived domains it has proven its worth in practice.

name: Lakehouse
description:
The lakehouse pattern collapses what used to be two stacks — a data lake for raw, semi-structured files and a data warehouse for curated, queryable tables — into a single architecture built on cheap object storage and open table formats. Formats such as Iceberg, Delta Lake and Apache Hudi layer ACID transactions, schema evolution, time travel and partition pruning on top of files in S3 Compatible Object Storage, while compute engines like Trino for interactive SQL and Spark for batch and streaming run independently against the same tables. The result is a shared, governed catalog that reporting, ML and operational analytics can all read from without first forcing the data through a parallel ETL pipeline.

We are placing lakehouse in assess because the building blocks are now mature enough to take seriously, but the operating model — catalog ownership, table compaction and retention, governance over who can write — is what determines whether a lakehouse stays clean or quietly degrades into a "data swamp with metadata". For teams currently splitting analytical data between an Oracle Database or Microsoft SQL Server warehouse, ad-hoc files on object storage and downstream copies in Elasticsearch or PostgreSQL, the pattern is worth piloting on a single bounded domain — pick one source of high-volume events, land it in Iceberg, and let one team consume it through Trino — before any commitment to it as a group-wide standard. What to validate is concurrent writer behavior for our actual ingestion patterns, query latency on representative dashboards, and the operational story for catalog backups, table maintenance and access control across tenants.

name: Multi-Agent Workflows
description:
Multi-agent workflows — what ThoughtWorks now describes as a team of coding agents — are an emerging way to tackle non-trivial coding tasks by orchestrating a small set of role-specific agents rather than relying on a single generalist. A primary orchestrator decomposes the work, sequences and parallelises subtasks, and the role-specific agents (for example a backend implementer, a frontend implementer and a reviewer) collaborate both with the orchestrator and with each other. Subagent support is rapidly becoming a baseline feature in coding tools, and recent releases such as Claude Code's agent teams provide built-in orchestration that lowers the barrier to trying this pattern.

It is worth being precise about scale. A deliberate team of a handful of agents is a very different beast from a fully autonomous swarm of dozens or hundreds of agents — the latter has a much higher entry cost, weaker quality signals and a different failure mode. In our context, "multi-agent" is closer to the team-of-agents end of the spectrum: small, well-defined roles, a human still on the loop, and clear hand-offs. Useful starting use cases are review/implement splits and clean backend/frontend separation; we recommend assessing it on a bounded internal task before reaching for swarm-scale orchestrations.

name: Product Context Pack
description:
A Product Context Pack packages a single product's complete knowledge — user guides, installation and operations documentation, API reference, business logic, database schemas and frontend code — into a vectorized, semantically searchable index that AI agents can query. The corpus is automatically chunked, embedded and refreshed as the product evolves, and is most commonly exposed through an MCP server so the same pack plugs into Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI and any other MCP-capable client a team already uses. When a user asks a question, the pack combines semantic similarity with keyword matching to surface the right chunks across documentation and source, and lets the AI client synthesize a grounded answer with citations back to the original files.

The value of the pattern is that every role around a product gets answers from the same source of truth. Sales and marketing pull benefit statements and feature descriptions for proposals; support and business analysts answer customer questions without digging through code; consultants and implementers find concrete setup and configuration steps; developers and system engineers get explanations backed by the actual implementation rather than just the manual. Because the index covers both written documentation and the codebase, a question like "how does retention policy work?" can return the user-facing concept, the business logic that evaluates it, the API endpoints that manage it and the database views that query it in one response.

This pattern picks up where the previous radar's AI for codebase Q&A assessment left off, narrowing the corpus to a single product but widening the audience — covering documentation alongside source code, and serving business roles, not only developers. We place it in Assess because we have an early internal implementation covering small number of products and want to validate the pattern more broadly: how to keep the index fresh as code changes, how to scope and govern access (especially to source code) per audience, and how to measure answer quality across roles. It builds directly on Context Engineering and Progressive Context Disclosure, and the cautions we raise in Agent Skills about defaulting to MCP still apply — for narrower, single-team needs a skill or local CLI is often the simpler fit.

name: Codebase Cognitive Debt
description:
Codebase cognitive debt is the growing gap between a system's implementation and a team's shared understanding of how and why it works. As AI increases change velocity, especially with multiple contributors or Multi-Agent Workflows, teams can lose track of design intent and hidden coupling. This, combined with rising technical debt, creates a reinforcing loop that makes systems progressively harder to reason about.

Weaker system understanding also reduces developer's ability to guide AI effectively, making it harder to anticipate edge cases and steer agents away from architectural pitfalls. Left unmanaged, teams reach a tipping point where small changes trigger unexpected failures, fixes introduce regressions and cleanup efforts increase risk instead of reducing it.

Teams should avoid complacency with AI-generated code and adopt explicit countermeasures: Feedback Loops for Agents, tracking team cognitive load and Architecture as Code to continuously enforce key constraints as AI accelerates output.

name: Cloud Native Storage
description: Cloud-native storage solutions have become critical components for running stateful applications in Kubernetes environments, providing persistent, scalable, and resilient storage that integrates seamlessly with container orchestration. We're seeing strong adoption of solutions like Rook-Ceph, which automates Ceph storage cluster deployment and management in Kubernetes, providing block, file, and S3-compatible object storage capabilities, and Longhorn, a lightweight distributed block storage system originally developed by Rancher. Other notable open-source alternatives include OpenEBS, which offers container-attached storage with multiple storage engines, and MinIO for object storage compatible with S3 APIs. These solutions provide flexibility and avoid vendor lock-in while delivering enterprise-grade features like replication, snapshots, and backup capabilities. For organizations preferring commercial support, solutions like Portworx offer advanced features including disaster recovery and data security, while Pure Storage Portworx provides enterprise-grade storage with comprehensive support and SLAs. We're placing cloud-native storage in adopt based on its maturity and necessity for production Kubernetes deployments. The key considerations are choosing the right solution based on workload requirements—block storage for databases, file storage for shared data, or object storage for unstructured data. Teams should evaluate performance requirements, operational complexity, and the trade-offs between self-managed open-source solutions and commercial offerings. Start with pilot projects to understand operational characteristics and ensure your team has the expertise to manage distributed storage systems. For organizations running stateful applications in Kubernetes, implementing a robust cloud-native storage solution is no longer optional but a fundamental requirement for production readiness.

name: Kafka
description: Apache Kafka provides a durable, high-throughput event log that decouples producers from consumers. Topics are partitioned for scale and replicated for fault tolerance, allowing independent services to publish and subscribe without direct knowledge of each other.Backpressure is handled naturally by consumer offsets, and replay is as simple as re-reading from an earlier offset. Schema enforcement with Avro or Protobuf protects compatibility, while compaction and retention policies align storage with business semantics. Common patterns include event-driven integration, change-data-capture pipelines, streaming ETL, and audit trails. Healthy clusters maintain in-sync replicas, even partition distribution, and predictable latency; observability centers on controller state, request timing, consumer lag, and under-replicated partitions. Exactly-once processing exists for narrow paths, yet most designs rely on idempotent producers and consumers for simplicity and resilience.

name: Keycloak
description: Keycloak is an open-source identity and access management solution that provides comprehensive authentication and authorization capabilities for modern applications. We've seen Keycloak mature into a robust platform that supports industry-standard protocols including OpenID Connect, OAuth 2.0, and SAML 2.0, making it suitable for both new applications and legacy system integration. The platform offers features like single sign-on (SSO), social login integration, user federation with LDAP/Active Directory, multi-factor authentication, and fine-grained authorization policies. Teams appreciate Keycloak's admin console for managing users, roles, and clients, along with its extensive customization options through themes and service provider interfaces. We're placing Keycloak in adopt based on its proven track record across our projects. It significantly reduces the complexity and development effort required to implement secure authentication and authorization, while providing enterprise-grade features out of the box. The main considerations are proper infrastructure sizing for high-availability deployments and understanding its operational requirements. Organizations should invest in learning Keycloak's realm and client configuration patterns, as proper setup is crucial for security and maintainability. For teams building applications that require authentication, Keycloak eliminates the need to build these capabilities from scratch and provides a battle-tested foundation for identity management.

name: Kubernetes
description:
Kubernetes is an orchestration platform that schedules and manages containerized workloads through declarative APIs. Deployments, StatefulSets, and Jobs describe desired state; the control plane reconciles actual state continuously. Service discovery, rolling updates, horizontal and vertical autoscaling, and self-healing provide robust day-to-day operations. A rich extension model—CRDs, operators, CSI for storage, CNI for networking, and Ingress/Gateway for traffic—supports diverse workloads from stateless web services to databases. Security and multi-tenancy benefit from namespaces, RBAC, network policies, and admission control. Effective clusters pair resource requests/limits with pod disruption budgets and readiness probes to enable safe rollouts. Observability integrates metrics, logs, and traces, commonly via Prometheus, centralized logging, and OpenTelemetry. Kubernetes standardizes deployment and runtime behavior across environments, enabling consistent delivery practices at scale.

Warning on microK8s: we have hit recurring operational issues (snap-driven upgrades, node recovery, addon lifecycle, HA edge cases) and do not recommend it for production until clarified. A meeting with Canonical is being scheduled to align on supported topologies and the recommended path forward.

name: Low CVE base images
description:
Adopting low CVE base images like Alpine Linux in your container deployments is a strategic shift toward improved security. This approach significantly reduces the attack surface and eliminates unnecessary components in containerized production environments, also minimizes the memory and disk requirements.

Implementation Strategy
Verify and audit current base images. Identify where container images are used. Using the base image add necessary components or choose an application specific image like java/nginx. Ensure all necessary dependencies are available in base package repositories

Application Notes Base images are minimal and do not contain the basic tools. If you are debugging the container, you may not find your network tool.

What options are available for low-CVE base images? 

Base Image                Size (MB)       Known CVEs (approx.)                Notes                                                            Alpine                    5-7             0-10 (minimal due to few packages)  very mature                                                     Alpaquita Linux           3-4             0-5 (Alpine + patching)             java optimized with BellSoft, free images, support commercial   Debian Slim               70-80           50-100 (mostly low-severity)        larger image                                                    Chainguard Wolfi (base)   1-15            0 (zero-CVE policy )                commercial general images, free tier available                                    BusyBox                   1-2             0-5 (ultra-minimal)                 no package manager, limited

Alpine Images are good enough with frequent updates. Commercial subscriptions can be considered for high compliance and customer facing environments.

name: NGINX
description:
NGINX is a high-performance HTTP server and reverse proxy widely used for load balancing, TLS termination, static content delivery, and as an edge gateway. It scales well with modest resource use, has a small operational footprint, and integrates smoothly with container orchestration and CI/CD pipelines.

When to use

  • Front your services with NGINX for reliable TLS termination and layer 7 routing.
  • Use as a performant static file server or as an ingress controller in Kubernetes.
  • Prefer NGINX when predictable high concurrency and low-latency routing are required.

Advice and trade-offs

  • Adopt default NGINX for most edge and proxy needs; use NGINX Plus only when enterprise features or vendor support are required.
  • Invest in secure default configs (rate limiting, header sanitization, TLS hardening) and automated config testing.
  • For advanced API gateway features consider combining with dedicated gateway solutions; for simple use-cases NGINX is often sufficient.

Kubernetes ingress controllers There are two well-supported, production-ready NGINX-based ingress controllers, and it is worth knowing they are distinct projects:

  • ingress-nginx (kubernetes/ingress-nginx): the community controller maintained under the Kubernetes project. It is the most widely deployed NGINX ingress in the wild, well-documented, and a solid default for most clusters.
  • NGINX Ingress Controller (nginxinc/kubernetes-ingress): maintained by NGINX/F5. It ships in two flavors — an open-source build on top of NGINX OSS and a commercial build on top of NGINX Plus. Beyond the standard Ingress API, it exposes its own CRDs (VirtualServer, VirtualServerRoute, TransportServer, Policy) for richer traffic management, supports dynamic reconfiguration without reloads, active health checks, JWT/OIDC authentication, and advanced load-balancing methods. The Plus variant adds commercial support and a real-time monitoring dashboard. Both are reasonable choices. Pick the community ingress-nginx for a familiar, broadly adopted default; pick the NGINX-provided controller when you want first-party CRDs, reload-free config updates, or the NGINX Plus feature set and support contract.

Resources

  • https://nginx.org
  • ingress-nginx (community): https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx
  • NGINX Ingress Controller (NGINX/F5): https://github.com/nginxinc/kubernetes-ingress
  • Migration patterns: reverse-proxy-first, gradual cutover, health-check-driven failover

name: PostgreSQL
description: PostgreSQL is an advanced open-source relational database system providing ACID guarantees, sophisticated query optimization, and extensive data type support including JSON, arrays, hstore, and custom types. The database offers powerful indexing strategies (B-tree, GiST, GIN, BRIN, hash), full-text search, window functions, CTEs, and advanced SQL features for complex analytical queries. PostgreSQL's extensibility through custom functions, operators, procedural languages (PL/pgSQL, PL/Python, PL/Java), and extensions like PostGIS for geospatial data, TimescaleDB for time-series, and pg_partman for partitioning enables specialized workloads. Robust concurrency control through MVCC, streaming replication, logical replication, and point-in-time recovery provide high availability and disaster recovery capabilities. Performance tuning involves query planning analysis with EXPLAIN, appropriate indexing strategies, connection pooling via PgBouncer, and configuration optimization for shared buffers, work memory, and WAL settings. Adopt PostgreSQL as the default relational database for applications requiring data integrity, complex queries, extensibility, and proven operational maturity across diverse workloads from transactional systems to analytical platforms.

name: Microsoft SQL Server
description:
Microsoft SQL Server is a robust, enterprise-grade relational database platform that offers extensive features for both development and production environments. Developers should adopt SQL Server because it provides seamless out-of-the-box integration with .NET applications, simplifying setup and data access during development. Its tooling, management studio, and support for local development make it easy to get started and maintain productivity.

For production, SQL Server delivers high reliability, scalability, advanced security features, and rich support for analytics, reporting, and high availability. SQL Server 2025 further strengthens this with optimized locking, Query Store improvements, tempdb space governance, ZSTD backup compression, TLS 1.3 support with TDS 8.0, and broader managed identity support. It is well-suited for mission-critical applications, offering comprehensive backup, monitoring, and performance tuning capabilities. With strong community and enterprise support, SQL Server remains a top choice for building and running modern data-driven applications.

SQL Server 2025 adds several features that make the platform more relevant for modern application workloads: native vector data types, vector indexes, and AI embedding functions for semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation scenarios; a native JSON data type with JSON aggregation support; regular expression and fuzzy string matching functions; and external REST endpoint invocation for integration with services such as Azure OpenAI.

name: ASEE Flow
description:
ASEE Flow is a drop-in replacement for Camunda 7 Community Edition, developed by ASEE to ensure continuity after Camunda 7 CE reached end-of-life in October 2025. It preserves full API, BPMN, and runtime compatibility with Camunda 7.24 (the final CE release), enabling seamless migration without code changes. ASEE Flow replaces the legacy Camunda Cockpit and Tasklist with a modern React JS-based interface providing improved process visibility and simplified troubleshooting.

The most important addition since the previous radar is the AI BPMN Assistant, which lets engineers and analysts collaborate with an LLM through a chat interface to design and refine BPMN processes. The LLM proposes the process, deterministic auto-layout code keeps the resulting diagram clean and editable rather than a one-off generation, and a built-in linter validates both standard BPMN correctness and product-specific rules — an instance of Agentic Engineering applied to BPMN authoring.

Already integrated into the ASEE Digital Platform BPM Microservice, ASEE Flow remains in trial as we evaluate operational characteristics across projects. With Camunda 7 CE support now ended, teams still using Camunda 7 CE directly — without Digital Platform — should migrate without further delay, testing in non-production environments first. For projects with significant investment in Camunda 7, ASEE Flow offers a low-risk path forward with maintained compatibility and ASEE-backed support.

name: Cassandra
description:
Apache Cassandra is a distributed, masterless wide-column NoSQL database built for big data workloads with extremely fast, scalable writes. Its peer-to-peer architecture, partitioned and replicated storage, and tunable consistency (per-query QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM, ONE, ALL) let teams scale horizontally across nodes and data centers while keeping predictable p99 write latency under heavy ingestion.
