Data is modeled query-first around partition and clustering keys, making Cassandra a strong fit for high-volume ingestion paths, event history, large-scale telemetry, and activity feeds where write throughput and continuous availability matter more than complex joins.

Cassandra is not a drop-in replacement for a relational database—there are no ad-hoc joins, transactions are limited to lightweight single-partition operations, and schema changes require care. Treat it as a purpose-built engine for write-heavy, scale-out workloads, and keep PostgreSQL or SQL Server as the default for transactional data.

name: Elasticsearch
description:
Elasticsearch is a distributed search and analytics engine built on Lucene. It shines for full-text search, application search, log analytics, and fast aggregations over large, time-ordered datasets. Data is indexed into shards and replicated across nodes for high availability and near-real-time queries. It is strongest where search relevance, Elastic ecosystem integrations, or managed Elastic capabilities justify the licensing and operating cost compared with open alternatives such as Open Search.

Use Elasticsearch where mature search relevance, ecosystem integrations, or Elastic-specific capabilities justify the platform choice. Before wider adoption, validate index and shard sizing, hot-warm-cold storage tiers, Index Lifecycle Management (ILM), snapshot/restore to S3-compatible storage, JVM/heap tuning, and ingestion pressure under realistic load. Elasticsearch is not a primary system of record; model for eventual consistency and design updates or deletes carefully.

name: Open Search
description:
OpenSearch is an open-source search and analytics engine derived from Elasticsearch, commonly used for full-text search, log analytics, dashboards, and operational investigation over large event streams. It is relevant when teams need Elasticsearch-like capabilities while avoiding Elastic licensing constraints or when they want a community-governed stack. Teams already using Elasticsearch should evaluate OpenSearch as a migration or new-workload option, not as a drop-in assumption.

Evaluate OpenSearch on bounded search or log analytics workloads before standardizing it. Validate API compatibility with existing Elasticsearch clients, index lifecycle and retention strategy, shard sizing, snapshot and restore to S3-compatible storage, security plugin configuration, and Kubernetes/operator maturity. For advanced observability use cases, compare it with the Grafana stack and commercial APM platforms, especially where traces, metrics, and logs must be correlated.

name: RabbitMQ
description:
RabbitMQ is an open-source messaging system based on the AMQP protocol that enables asynchronous communication between distributed components. It is widely used to decouple services and manage message queues reliably.

RabbitMQ is a mature, stable technology with a strong ecosystem, making it ideal for microservices architectures or systems requiring resilience and concurrent processing. Its implementation can enhance scalability and fault tolerance. It is particularly suitable for work queue patterns due to its robust messaging and persistence capabilities.

For architectures that need to handle continuous, large-scale event streams—such as event streaming or data analytics systems, Kafka may be a more appropriate choice. A validation phase against alternatives such as Kafka or Azure Service Bus is recommended, assessing message nature, persistence requirements, and expected throughput.

name: S3 Compatible Object Storage
description:
Object storage manages data as objects with metadata and unique identifiers, in contrast to hierarchical file systems or block storage. S3, AWS's object storage service, has become the de facto standard, and its API is widely implemented by cloud providers and storage vendors — making it a portable foundation rather than a vendor-specific commitment.

When to Use It

S3-compatible object storage is well suited to unstructured data accessed over HTTP at scale: data lakes, backups and archives, ML training datasets, log retention, static web assets, and large media. It is generally a poor fit for low-latency transactional workloads or anything that needs POSIX semantics — block storage or a managed file system will serve those better. Be aware of the trade-offs: higher per-operation latency than block storage, eventual consistency in some implementations, and a cost model driven by request count and egress rather than provisioned capacity.

Landscape Considerations

For cloud-native deployments, Cloud Native Storage provide S3-compatible object storage for Kubernetes environments. The open-source landscape has shifted notably: MinIO, previously a default choice, has scaled back its community edition — most web console features were removed and AGPL terms are being enforced more aggressively, prompting many teams to reassess. This underscores the importance of evaluating licensing stability, vendor lock-in risk, and long-term community governance when picking an implementation. RustFS is an emerging alternative worth monitoring, though still early. Prioritize solutions with transparent, stable licensing to preserve operational independence.

Adoption Recommendation

S3-compatible object storage is worth piloting as the standard for unstructured data, with implementation chosen to fit the deployment context. For cloud-native environments, evaluate open-source options carefully against the licensing concerns above. For enterprise on-prem setups, Hitachi Content Platform is one mature option — it supports Virtual Appliance, dedicated hardware, and multitenant deployments, which can be useful where resource isolation and independent billing across tenants matter. Choose based on workload profile, deployment constraints, and the licensing posture you can live with long-term.

name: Spark
description:
Apache Spark is a mature distributed data processing engine for large-scale batch ETL, stream processing, machine learning pipelines, and data transformations that exceed the practical limits of a single database or application service. It is a proven standard for data-heavy workloads, but it also brings operational complexity, resource tuning, and cost management responsibilities that teams should understand before making it the default.

Use Spark when workloads require parallel processing across large datasets, especially in lakehouse architectures using Iceberg, S3 Compatible Object Storage, and SQL engines such as Trino. Avoid introducing Spark for small scheduled jobs, simple reporting queries, or transformations that can run reliably inside PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, or lightweight pipeline solutions. Validate execution environment, job orchestration, observability, retry behavior, data skew, and developer experience for maintaining jobs over time.

name: Bun
description: Bun is a JavaScript and TypeScript runtime, package manager, bundler and test runner built on JavaScriptCore and a native toolchain written in Zig. It targets the same workloads as Node.js but ships them as a single fast binary: bun install, bun run and bun test, with a built-in bundler and transpiler that handle TypeScript and JSX out of the box. Compatibility with the Node.js API surface and npm registry is a primary design goal, so most existing packages and scripts work unchanged. We are putting it in Assess because the headline benefits—much faster install and startup times, native TypeScript, and a unified toolchain—are visible on day one, but the production track record inside our portfolio is still limited. Anywhere we already run Node.js (services, scripts, build tooling, developer CLIs) Bun is worth evaluating; what to validate is API compatibility for the specific Node libraries we depend on (native addons, streams, framework integrations), production stability and observability (profiling, OpenTelemetry, APM agents), and behaviour under realistic load. Until at least one non-trivial workload runs on Bun in production, Node.js remains the default and Bun is a deliberate, scoped experiment alongside it.

name: Cillium
description:
Cilium is an eBPF-based CNI for Kubernetes that replaces traditional iptables-driven networking with kernel-level data planes for Pod connectivity, Service load balancing, NetworkPolicy enforcement and observability. Because rules are compiled to eBPF and applied directly in the kernel, Cilium scales policy and service handling far better than iptables under high pod churn or large service counts, and exposes rich L3/L4 and L7-aware policies (HTTP, gRPC, Kafka) without sidecars. Hubble ships with it as a flow-level observability layer — every packet, drop and policy decision is visible by workload identity rather than by IP, which is a noticeable step up from what we get from a default CNI today. Beyond networking, Cilium also offers a sidecar-less service mesh and transparent encryption (WireGuard or IPsec), positioning it as an alternative to running a full Istio stack for many use cases. It can replace also ingress controller in Kubernetes cluster with a limitation related to passthrough SSL communication which is not supported.

We are placing Cilium in assess because eBPF is the direction the Kubernetes ecosystem is clearly moving and the security and observability story is genuinely compelling, but adopting it touches the most sensitive layer of a cluster and demands a clear migration plan. What to validate is kernel version requirements across our distributions and managed Kubernetes offerings (eBPF features depend on a recent enough kernel), behavior of existing NetworkPolicies under Cilium semantics, performance on east-west traffic for our microservices workloads, and the operational story for upgrades, debugging dropped flows and integrating Hubble with our Grafana stack. Before any production move, run it on a non-critical cluster and compare against the current CNI on real workloads — the headline benefits only matter if they survive contact with our actual traffic patterns.

name: Iceberg
description:
Apache Iceberg is an open table format that brings database-like guarantees to data stored in object stores and data lakes. It supports schema evolution, partition evolution, snapshots, time travel, and safer concurrent writes, making it attractive for lakehouse architectures where multiple engines need to read and write the same analytical tables. The architectural benefits are strong, but adoption requires clear ownership of catalogs, compaction, retention, and governance.

Evaluate Iceberg together with Spark, Trino, S3 Compatible Object Storage, and a lakehouse operating model rather than as a standalone technology. It is a good fit for analytical datasets that need long-term evolution, reproducibility, and engine interoperability. It is not a replacement for transactional relational databases such as PostgreSQL or Microsoft SQL Server. Teams should validate catalog choice, access control, small-file handling, snapshot cleanup, backup strategy, and query performance on representative data.

name: Istio
description:
Istio is a Kubernetes service mesh that adds traffic management, mutual TLS, authorization policy, retries, canary routing, and service-to-service observability without pushing all of that logic into application code. Its capabilities are valuable for complex, security-sensitive microservice platforms, but the operational and cognitive cost is significant. Teams should consider Istio only when those service-to-service controls are clearly needed, not just because they run Kubernetes.

Evaluate Istio when a system has many services, strict zero-trust or compliance requirements, frequent progressive delivery needs, or a clear need for mesh-level telemetry and policy. For simpler systems, prefer well-configured ingress, API gateways, network policies, and application-level resilience before adding a mesh. A pilot should validate sidecar or ambient mode, performance overhead, certificate lifecycle, debugging workflows, integration with OpenTelemetry SDKs, and whether alternatives such as Linkerd or Cilium service mesh would be easier to operate.

name: Micro VM Runtimes
description: Micro VM container runtimes (Firecracker, Kata Containers, Cloud Hypervisor) run each container inside a lightweight virtual machine instead of sharing the host kernel. They keep the OCI/CRI interfaces and Kubernetes integration that operators already know, but trade a small amount of startup time and density for hardware-level isolation, a much smaller attack surface than shared-kernel runtimes, and stronger noisy-neighbour guarantees. Boot times in the tens to low hundreds of milliseconds and per-VM memory overhead in the low tens of MB make them practical for general workloads, not just specialised ones. We treat this as a category rather than a single product: the right choice depends on the workload (Firecracker for fast, minimal serverless-style isolation; Kata for drop-in OCI/Kubernetes use; Cloud Hypervisor where richer device support matters). We are putting it in Assess to evaluate it for multi-tenant clusters, untrusted code paths (CI runners, customer-supplied workloads, plugin/agent execution), and regulated environments where stronger isolation is a hard requirement; what to validate is performance overhead on representative workloads, integration with our Kubernetes distributions and CNI/CSI choices, image and kernel lifecycle management, and the operational story for debugging, observability and incident response.

name: Redis
description: Redis is our low-latency accelerator for caching, counters, lightweight queues, sessions, and rate limits—not a source of truth. We run it on Kubernetes with an operator and treat placement as a resilience tool: leaders are spread, followers are kept on different nodes, and pods are balanced to avoid single-node risk. The main lessons are conceptual: design for bounded memory so structures never grow without limits; choose a sensible eviction strategy and avoid wide, blocking scans. Optimize client behavior by pooling connections, batching with pipelining, and reducing hot-key contention. Keep production safe with strict command hygiene and access control, preferring iterative scans over risky commands. Be intentional about persistence, selecting cache-only or append-only/snapshot modes based on recovery needs rather than habit. Build in security and isolation from the start, and observe everything—latency, throughput, memory health, replication—so drift triggers timely alerts. Finally, codify these practices in scheduling rules, resource sizing, and simple restore drills to keep Redis fast, predictable, and boring.

name: Trino
description:
Trino (formerly PrestoSQL) is a highly parallel and distributed SQL query engine designed for fast, interactive analytics over data that lives outside a traditional database — object storage, lakehouse tables, relational engines, message logs — without first copying it into a warehouse. A coordinator plans queries, workers execute them in parallel against pluggable connectors, and the engine's strength is federation: a single SQL query can join an Iceberg table on object storage with a transactional table in PostgreSQL and a topic in Kafka, which is exactly the shape of question that today usually triggers a bespoke ETL job. Compute is decoupled from storage, so clusters can be scaled horizontally for query concurrency and turned off when idle.

We are placing Trino in assess as the natural query layer for the Lakehouse pattern and as a candidate for ad-hoc analytics across our existing systems of record. The headline value is opening up data already on S3 Compatible Object Storage to SQL users without a separate warehouse, but the practical questions are operational: catalog and access management across many connectors, memory and concurrency tuning, query cost control under multi-tenant use, and how to keep dashboards stable when source systems change. Trino is not a system of record and not a substitute for Spark on heavy batch transformations — pick it where interactive latency over large, cold data matters, and validate first that one realistic dashboard workload survives a representative day of concurrent users before investing in a wider rollout.

name: Victoria Traces
description: Victoria Traces is an open-source distributed tracing backend from the VictoriaMetrics family, designed as a lightweight, resource-efficient alternative to heavier tracing stacks. It ingests traces over standard protocols (OTLP, Jaeger), stores them in a compact columnar format, and integrates with familiar query and visualisation surfaces. Like Victoria Metrics and Victoria Logs, it emphasises a low memory footprint, a simple single-binary operational model, and predictable cost at scale. We are putting it in Assess because we already operate Victoria Metrics in production—if Victoria Traces delivers comparable economics for trace storage and query, it gives us a unified observability stack (metrics, logs, traces) under one operational paradigm instead of running parallel Jaeger/Tempo/Elasticsearch deployments. Validate it on a real workload first: ingest throughput and storage cost, query performance for trace search and service maps, integration with our OpenTelemetry collectors and Grafana dashboards, and the maturity of retention, downsampling and tenancy controls.

name: ActiveMQ Artemis
description:
ActiveMQ Artemis is a performant, feature-rich message broker implementing JMS 2.0 with support for AMQP, MQTT, STOMP, and OpenWire. It offers high throughput, low latency, and flexible configuration for enterprise messaging workloads.

We place Artemis in the Hold ring primarily due to persistent operational challenges in Kubernetes and cloud-native environments. Artemis’s architecture depends on shared state and journal-based persistence, which conflicts with stateless, horizontally scalable design principles. Setting up high availability (HA) requires complex coordination using shared file systems or replicated databases, which are brittle under container orchestration. Moreover, Artemis lacks native autoscaling, operator maturity, and observability integrations compared to modern distributed logs or streaming platforms.

For new workloads, teams should prefer brokers designed from the ground up for partitioned, state-distributed operation with stronger Kubernetes support and operational simplicity such as Kafka or RedPanda. Artemis remains viable for legacy JMS integration but unsuitable as a cloud-native backbone.

name: Internet Information Services
description:
Internet Information Services (IIS) is Microsoft’s long-standing web server for hosting web applications and services on Windows. It integrates tightly with the Windows ecosystem and supports ASP.NET, .NET Core, PHP, and other frameworks, providing features such as application pools, SSL/TLS, URL rewriting, and diagnostics tools. Historically, IIS served as the backbone of enterprise .NET hosting and intranet deployments.

However, we have placed IIS in the Hold ring due to its inherent incompatibility with cloud-native and containerized architectures. Its dependency on the Windows platform makes it difficult to deploy, scale, and maintain within Kubernetes environments. Configurations rely on stateful system management rather than declarative infrastructure, limiting automation and portability. Additionally, it carries higher resource overhead and Windows licensing costs.

Modern workloads should standardize on Kestrel (for .NET) or NGINX as lightweight, cross-platform web servers that align with containerized, cloud-native practices and deliver simpler scaling and operational models.

name: Oracle Database
description:
Oracle Database remains one of the most capable enterprise RDBMS platforms, offering advanced HA, clustering, partitioning, and security features. Technically, it delivers strong performance, rich SQL and PL/SQL capabilities, and proven reliability for mission-critical workloads. It offers advanced features such as ACID compliance, multitenant architecture (CDB/PDB), Real Application Clusters (RAC) for high availability, and Data Guard for disaster recovery.

We have placed Oracle Database in the Hold ring due to its high total cost of ownership (TCO) and limited compatibility with modern development ecosystems. Integration with modern ecosystems (Kubernetes, Kafka, observability, CI/CD pipelines) is cumbersome, while vendor lock-in limits cloud portability. Several ASEE projects have faced challenging contract negotiations and restrictive licensing that negatively impacted our timelines and revenue.

We recommend PostgreSQL and Microsoft SQL Server as strategic alternatives that balance functionality, ecosystem integration, and supportability. Existing Oracle workloads should be maintained but no new systems should adopt it unless mandated by client constraints.

name: VMware vSphere
description:
VMware vSphere is an enterprise virtualization platform providing comprehensive capabilities for running virtual machines and managing data center infrastructure. While vSphere has been a dominant solution with proven stability, Broadcom's acquisition of VMware has disrupted the market with dramatic price increases and licensing model changes, forcing organizations to reconsider their virtualization strategies.

Broadcom shifted to subscription-only models with substantial price hikes, bundled previously separate products, and eliminated lower-tier editions. This has accelerated interest in alternatives like Proxmox, OpenStack, and Kubernetes. ASEE is focusing new projects on Kubernetes for cloud-native infrastructure, aligning with industry trends toward container orchestration. We're placing VMware vSphere in hold, recommending teams pause new vSphere investments. Existing deployments should continue operating while assessing migration paths. For new infrastructure projects, teams should prioritize Kubernetes-based solutions with Cloud Native Storage unless specific vSphere dependencies justify the increased investment.

name: AI coding assistants
description:
AI coding assistants such as GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code, and others are reshaping how developers write, understand, and maintain code. These tools go beyond simple autocomplete; they serve as conversational partners that can generate functions, suggest refactorings, write tests, explain code, or summarize large repositories. Many teams in our group report positive experience using AI assistants to reduce boilerplate, speed up debugging, and improve test coverage. Teams should use first opportunity to introduce use of AI coding assistants into their workflow.

Integrated within IDEs or terminals, they support pair-programming workflows and accelerate onboarding by helping engineers query complex legacy systems conversationally. However, productivity gains come with governance and risk management requirements—avoiding sensitive data exposure, IP contamination, or over-reliance on unreviewed output. Other notable tools include JetBrains AI Assistant, Amazon CodeWhisperer, Tabnine, and Codeium.

name: Containers and K8S on dev machine
description:
Containers and Kubernetes on development machines represent a mature and proven approach to cloud-native development, enabling teams to build and test software in production-like environments locally. This practice bridges the gap between development and production by allowing developers to run containerized applications, debug Kubernetes manifests, and validate infrastructure-as-code changes in isolated setups.

The ecosystem has evolved beyond traditional Docker Desktop. Rancher Desktop provides a stable, lightweight Kubernetes distribution with built-in container runtime support, while Podman offers a daemonless, Docker-compatible engine that integrates cleanly with kind and minikube for local cluster management. Compose-style setups remain useful for simple dependencies, but local Kubernetes delivers closer alignment with production orchestration models.

Teams adopting this approach benefit from improved environment consistency and faster feedback cycles. However, running full Kubernetes locally can be resource-intensive and may differ from managed cloud clusters in networking and storage behavior. Emerging options such as Dev Containers and GitHub Codespaces are extending these concepts to cloud-hosted development environments.

Learn more in the official Kubernetes documentation.

name: GitHub
description: GitHub is the leading platform for Git repository hosting and code collaboration, providing pull requests for code review, issue tracking, project management, CI/CD automation via GitHub Actions, package management, and security scanning with Dependabot and CodeQL. The platform's pull request workflow with draft PRs, suggested changes, automated checks, required reviews, and branch protection rules has become the industry standard for maintaining code quality. GitHub Actions offers powerful CI/CD with marketplace integrations, while security features include secret scanning and dependency vulnerability alerts. Integration with IDEs and development tools is ubiquitous, and the platform hosts the world's largest open-source community. GitHub Enterprise provides SSO, audit logs, advanced security policies, and self-hosted deployment options for compliance requirements. Adopt GitHub as the primary platform for source code management and collaboration across all project sizes.

name: Gitlab CI/CD
description:
GitLab CI/CD is a powerful, built-in Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery system that is a core part of the GitLab DevOps platform. It automates the entire software delivery process—from building and testing to deploying and monitoring—using a simple, version-controlled YAML configuration file (.gitlab-ci.yml) stored alongside your code. It utilizes Runners to execute jobs, supporting complex workflows like parallel execution, caching, and integrated security scanning (DevSecOps), all within the same environment as your Git repository.

GitLab CI/CD represents a mature, low-friction standard for setting up modern development pipelines. For new projects, adopting a mature CI/CD system from day one is mandatory for maintaining a healthy codebase and high development velocity. The key advantage of GitLab CI/CD is its single-platform integration: you don't need to install, integrate, or maintain separate CI servers and source control. This significantly reduces setup overhead and the likelihood of toolchain issues. The YAML syntax is widely understood, and the platform provides excellent templates and auto-DevOps features, making it the default choice to ensure a reliable, automated pipeline is active from the very first commit.

name: GitLab
description: GitLab is a comprehensive DevOps platform that provides source code management, CI/CD pipelines, container registry, security scanning, and project management capabilities in a single application. We've consistently observed GitLab's evolution from a GitHub alternative into a complete DevOps lifecycle tool that reduces toolchain complexity and integration overhead. The platform's built-in CI/CD with GitLab Runners, merge request workflows, and Auto DevOps features enable teams to implement modern software delivery practices without stitching together multiple tools. GitLab's security features including SAST, DAST, dependency scanning, and container scanning are particularly valuable for organizations with compliance requirements. Both self-hosted and SaaS options provide flexibility for different organizational needs, with the self-hosted option offering greater control over data and infrastructure. We're placing GitLab in adopt based on widespread successful implementations across our projects. It delivers significant value through reduced tool sprawl, unified visibility across the development lifecycle, and strong CI/CD capabilities. Teams should be prepared for GitLab's comprehensive feature set, which can be overwhelming initially — start with core Git workflows and gradually adopt additional features. Organizations already invested in other DevOps toolchains should evaluate migration costs carefully, but for new projects or teams looking to consolidate their tooling, GitLab provides an excellent all-in-one solution.

name: Harbor
description:
Harbor is a production-ready, open-source container registry that adds RBAC, image signing, vulnerability scanning, replication and Helm/OCI support on top of a Docker distribution. We recommend adopting Harbor for organisation-wide registries and CI/CD workflows that need centralized scanning and policy enforcement; note it requires backing services (database, Redis, object storage) and operational care for backups, TLS, and upgrades.

References: https://goharbor.io/ — https://goharbor.io/docs/

name: Helm
description:
Helm is the de facto package manager for Kubernetes. It packages Kubernetes resources as charts, supports versioned releases, lifecycle upgrades/rollbacks, and chart discovery via repositories/OCI registries. Helm is tool for everyday DevOps

Why now

  • Mature ecosystem, wide adoption, strong tooling (linting, testing, artifact registries). Charts speed reproducible installs and simplify complex templates for teams deploying many services.

When to use

  • Use Helm to standardize and templatize Kubernetes deployments, manage upgrades and rollbacks, and distribute curated, versioned operational patterns across teams.

Caveats / Considerations

  • Templating complexity can grow; prefer small focused charts and clear values.yaml.
  • Pay attention to chart provenance, signed charts or OCI registry controls, and secret handling (avoid embedding secrets in values).
  • For GitOps workflows consider combining Helm with a GitOps controller (Argo CD, Flux) or evaluate Kustomize if you prefer pure overlays.

name: Jira
description:
Jira is a premier software development management platform from Atlassian. Originally a bug tracker, it has evolved into a comprehensive tool for Agile project management that supports Scrum, Kanban, and custom methodologies. Jira's core function is to organize, track, and manage work items (Issues)—including user stories, tasks, and bugs—through customizable workflows. It offers features like backlogs, sprint boards, roadmaps, reporting (e.g., burndown charts), and extensive APIs/integrations, making it a central hub for development, testing, and even non-technical teams.

Jira is a excellent pick when starting new projects, as establishing clear work tracking is foundational to Agile Development delivery. Adopting Jira early provides immediate process standardization and visibility. It's the industry standard for professional software teams, meaning it minimizes the learning curve for new hires and integrates seamlessly with nearly every other popular development tool (GitHub, GitLab, Gitlab CI/CD, etc.). By using it from Day 1, you instantly gain a single source of truth for requirements, progress, and historical data, which is essential for effective sprint planning, stakeholder communication, and post-release analysis.

name: Mermaid
description:
Mermaid is a powerful JavaScript-based diagramming tool that allows you to generate diagrams and charts from simple, Markdown-inspired text definitions (Diagrams as Code). Instead of using a graphical editor, you define the structure of a diagram—such as a flowchart, sequence diagram, class diagram, or Gantt chart—using a readable text syntax. The library then renders this text into a visual, vector-based diagram (typically SVG) that can be easily displayed in web browsers or documentation.

Mermaid solves a fundamental problem: Documentation Rot. Traditional image-based diagrams quickly become outdated as a project evolves and are tedious to update and impossible to version control effectively. By adopting Mermaid, diagrams become text-based assets that are stored alongside the source code. This aligns with the "documentation as code" principle, allowing diagrams to be version-controlled, reviewed via Pull Requests, and automatically rendered in tools like GitHub, GitLab, and most wiki/documentation platforms. This dramatically reduces the friction and cost of keeping technical diagrams accurate, ensuring that documentation remains a reliable and valuable resource from a project's inception.

name: Postman
description:
Postman is an established API development and testing platform that has consistently proven its value across ASEE teams and projects. It streamlines the design, documentation, and validation of APIs through an intuitive interface for crafting requests, managing environments, and automating test scripts. Its strong support for REST, GraphQL, and SOAP APIs, along with built-in mocking, monitoring, and documentation capabilities, makes it a comprehensive solution for end-to-end API lifecycle management.

We place Postman in the Adopt ring based on positive, widespread experience across multiple teams. It has demonstrated high usability, reliability, and effective collaboration through shared collections and workspaces.

Beyond manual exploration, Postman collections become a first-class step in automated API testing within DevOps workflows when executed headlessly in CI/CD pipelines via Newman, Postman's official command-line runner that executes the same collections and test scripts authored in the UI without rewriting them. Teams wire Newman into Gitlab CI/CD, GitHub Actions or Azure DevOps as a dedicated API test stage, with version-controlled collections and environments producing machine-readable reports (e.g. newman-reporter-htmlextra or JUnit XML) that feed Test Reporting dashboards and reinforce quality and consistency across releases. The same collections can be reused with K6 for performance follow-ups and ZAP (OWASP ZAP) for security scans, extending coverage without duplicating test assets.

For our group, Postman for authoring and Newman for pipeline execution turns API tests into a reliable quality gate that catches regressions and contract changes before deployment, and its maturity and adoption rate make it the pragmatic, standard choice for API design, testing and cross-team interoperability.

name: Shared credentials management
description:
Centralised credentials and secret management provides secure storage, fine-grained access control, rotation and auditability for the secrets used by applications and platform components. It decouples secret lifecycle from application code, removes long-lived credentials from manifests and pipelines, and is now a de facto standard enterprise practice driven by security, compliance and multi-cloud/Kubernetes adoption.

We are moving this blip to Adopt and recommending HashiCorp Vault as the standard backend for teams across the group. Vault gives us a mature, well-understood platform for organisation-wide secrets, cross-team reuse, automated rotation and dynamic, short-lived credentials, with strong audit trails. For Kubernetes workloads, integrate Vault through external-secrets or a CSI provider rather than embedding long-lived secrets in manifests, and apply least-privilege policies from day one. Plan for the operational realities—HA, backups, secret leasing, secure injection patterns—and avoid over-broad roles, secret sprawl, and high-cardinality telemetry on secret access. References: https://www.vaultproject.io/ — https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/secret/ — External Secrets operators (external-secrets.io)

name: Trivy
description:
Trivy is a comprehensive, open-source security scanner for containers, Kubernetes, infrastructure-as-code, and more. It has emerged as the de-facto standard for scanning container images, offering fast and reliable vulnerability detection with minimal configuration overhead. Trivy supports multiple sources (OS packages, language-specific dependencies, config files) and integrates easily into CI/CD workflows and developer tooling.

Beyond vulnerability scanning, Trivy also supports Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) generation, helping teams meet compliance, transparency, and traceability requirements for modern software supply chains. Its native support for SBOM formats such as SPDX and CycloneDX enables further tooling interoperability and regulatory alignment.

We place Trivy in the Adopt ring due to its high usability, active development, and proven effectiveness in real-world use. Its broad protocol support, reliable results, and seamless DevSecOps integration make it a pragmatic choice for container security at scale. Trivy should be part of the standard toolkit for secure software delivery.

name: ZAP (OWASP ZAP)
description:
ZAP (Zed Attack Proxy) is a free, open source tool for Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) and the de-facto standard in this domain. Part of the OWASP ecosystem, ZAP is one of the most widely used web application security scanners worldwide. It can find vulnerabilities in web applications and APIs by automatically crawling endpoints and scanning for issues like injection vulnerabilities, security misconfigurations, and other common security flaws.

ZAP offers both passive scanning (observing traffic for vulnerabilities) and active scanning (automated attacks on targets), backed by a rich set of plugins and an automation-friendly design. Teams in our organization use ZAP for API security testing and have scripted its REST API for integration into CI/CD pipelines. This allows developers to include ZAP scans in build or deployment workflows, performing continuous security checks without significant manual effort. So far, we have not encountered any notable limitations in ZAP’s capabilities, which speaks to its maturity and reliability as a go-to DAST solution.

We recommend moved OWASP ZAP from the Trial ring to the Adopt ring based on our positive internal experience, its proven value in improving application security, and the fact that it is a well-established and standardized tool in the security testing domain.

This move is also supported by the increasing regulatory focus on cybersecurity, secure software development, and continuous security testing. Regulations and frameworks such as DORA, CRA, and similar initiatives will require organizations to demonstrate stronger security controls, vulnerability management, and testing practices across the software development lifecycle.

For this reason, OWASP ZAP should not be treated only as an optional or experimental tool, but as a standard part of secure development practices. We recommend integrating ZAP into the software development lifecycle (SDLC) and aligning its usage with secure software development frameworks such as SSDF. This may include running automated ZAP scans as part of regular development, CI/CD, and QA processes.

By embedding ZAP into delivery pipelines, teams can identify vulnerabilities earlier, improve remediation speed, and strengthen a security-first mindset throughout the development process.

name: GitHub Actions
description:
GitHub Actions is a continuous integration and continuous delivery platform that automates build, test, security scanning, release, and deployment workflows directly from GitHub repositories. It provides a rich ecosystem of pre-built actions through the GitHub Marketplace, supports reusable workflows across repositories, and integrates with GitHub pull requests, environments, secrets, and branch protection rules.

Use GitHub Actions for teams already hosting code on GitHub, especially when automation needs to stay close to pull requests, repository events, and release workflows. Start with bounded pipelines and clear guardrails: pin third-party actions, define a runner strategy, integrate Shared credentials management, and monitor build minutes and storage cost. Reusable workflows should be centralized for common build, test, and release patterns so teams avoid copying fragile YAML across repositories. Teams standardized on GitLab should keep Gitlab CI/CD as the default unless there is a strong repository or ecosystem reason to split CI/CD platforms.

name: Grafana stack
description:
Modern observability stacks have become essential for understanding system behavior in distributed architectures, providing unified visibility across metrics, logs, and traces — the three pillars of observability. The Grafana observability stack, combining Grafana Loki for logs, Tempo for traces, and Mimir or Prometheus for metrics, represents a compelling open-source alternative for infrastructure monitoring (IM) and application performance monitoring (APM). We're seeing increased interest in this unified approach as teams seek to consolidate their observability tooling while maintaining flexibility and cost control. The stack's strength lies in its integration—correlated metrics, logs, and traces within a single interface significantly improve troubleshooting efficiency compared to disparate tools. Grafana's rich visualization capabilities and extensive plugin ecosystem enable teams to build comprehensive dashboards tailored to their specific needs.

Placed in trial as the stack has matured inside the group: production deployments across multiple teams have validated the integration, the operational story around deployment, tuning and retention is well understood, and correlated metrics, logs and traces have repeatedly proven their value during real incidents. Solid enough now to recommend as the default open-source observability foundation. Teams evaluating alternatives like Elastic Observability, Dynatrace or IBM Instana should treat the Grafana stack as the baseline and justify deviations against it. The main considerations remain operational overhead of running multiple components, LogQL and PromQL learning curves, and scaling at very high data volumes.

name: Playwright
description:
Playwright is a modern end-to-end (E2E) testing framework for web apps that automates real browsers—Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit—with one API. It ships with a test runner, auto-waiting actions, resilient locators, network mocking, screenshots/videos, and a trace viewer. Teams use it to validate critical user flows, catch regressions across browsers, and debug flaky UI behavior with rich artifacts.

The tool has moved to Trial status because the initial feedback was positive and its feature set appears to meet several important requirements for our testing strategy. In particular, Playwright provides good support for automated UI testing in CI pipelines, parallel test execution, isolated browser contexts, authentication fixtures, retries, API testing, file upload/download handling, permissions, mobile emulation, and browser-level debugging. These features justify deeper technical validation in a controlled trial phase.

During the Trial phase, the focus should be on testing Playwright against real project scenarios, including authentication flows, dashboard navigation, form submission, role-based access, file handling, and other high-value business processes. The trial should also evaluate test stability, execution time in pipelines, maintainability of test scripts, reporting quality, artifact collection, and integration with our existing CI/CD and development workflow.

Although Playwright offers strong capabilities, UI tests are still slower and more expensive to maintain than unit or integration tests. It should not be treated as a replacement for lower-level testing, nor as a load or performance testing tool. The trial should therefore also define clear usage boundaries, such as using Playwright mainly for critical user flows rather than creating excessive end-to-end coverage.

Based on the positive assessment results, Playwright is considered a strong candidate for adoption, but final approval depends on the outcome of deeper testing during the Trial phase. Best practices to validate during the trial include stable locators such as data-testid, per-test isolation, deterministic test data, controlled timeouts, limited retries, and collection of screenshots, videos, and traces on failure.

name: SonarQube
description:
SonarQube is a code quality and security analysis platform that automatically scans source code for bugs, vulnerabilities, code smells, and security hotspots. Its comprehensive detection of both quality and security issues makes it attractive for maintaining high code standards and reducing security risks. SonarQube supports over 30 programming languages and integrates seamlessly with CI/CD pipelines.

ASEE hosts the Enterprise Edition on ASEE Cloud, which is the preferred usage model providing advanced features like branch analysis, security reports, and portfolio management. Community Edition (open-source) and SonarCloud (SaaS) are available alternatives. Already integrated into the Secure Development Framework, we're placing SonarQube in trial as we evaluate its effectiveness in identifying vulnerabilities and enforcing quality standards across projects, particularly for Spring Boot and other Java applications. For teams prioritizing security and code quality, SonarQube provides automated, consistent enforcement that manual reviews alone cannot achieve.

SonarQube remains a key part of our AI development practice — not something to bypass because the agent already reviewed its own output. Its objective findings on bugs, vulnerabilities and duplication are exactly the Feedback Loops for Agents we want around the workflow in AI for development: findings the agent must respect, regardless of which model wrote the code.

name: Test management tools
description:
Test management tools such as TestRail, Zephyr, qTest, and Azure Test Plans help organize, track, and manage the testing process throughout the software development lifecycle. These platforms provide centralized hubs for test planning, execution, reporting, and collaboration among team members, improving test organization and traceability across complex projects.

Most tools integrate seamlessly with Jira, GitHub, Azure DevOps, CI/CD pipelines, and automation frameworks like Selenium or Playwright, making them valuable for projects with multiple testers and complex test scenarios. They offer comprehensive metrics, traceability matrices, and customizable dashboards that help maintain test coverage and quality metrics. However, teams should consider the additional tooling overhead, learning curve, and cost implications for enterprise features. Some tools are already being used successfully within the group, demonstrating their value for improving collaboration between testers and developers.

name: Agentic workflow tools
description: Agentic workflow tools orchestrate AI systems that autonomously plan, execute, and iterate on multi-step tasks via reasoning, tool use, and memory. Modern stacks include graph/state orchestrators like LangGraph and LlamaIndex Workflows, multi-agent frameworks like CrewAI and OpenAI Agents SDK (evolved from Swarm), and enterprise/low-code options such as n8n AI Agents and platform kits like OpenAI AgentKit. These tools power patterns like repo-wide refactoring, self-correcting test generation, incident triage, knowledge-base synthesis, and long-running build troubleshooting. Risks remain: flaky autonomy, complex debugging/observability, permissions & data-safety, and runaway costs from deep call-chains. Assess for bounded internal use (developer tooling, data/ops pipelines) with human-in-the-loop controls, clear rollback paths, spend guards, and production telemetry before placing on critical paths.

name: Appium
description:
Appium is an open-source automation framework for testing native, hybrid, and mobile web applications on Android and iOS. It uses the WebDriver protocol and allows teams to write tests in common programming languages while exercising real application behavior on emulators, simulators, and physical devices.

We are placing Appium in assess because it is a strong candidate for mobile test automation, but successful adoption depends heavily on the surrounding execution model. Teams should validate device-lab availability, emulator and simulator stability, CI/CD integration, parallel execution, test data setup, selector strategy, and reporting through tools such as Test Reporting or Report Portal. Appium is complementary to browser-focused tools such as Playwright; it should be evaluated for mobile app flows where real device capabilities, platform APIs, permissions, and native UI behavior matter.

During assessment, teams should start with a narrow set of critical journeys and measure test reliability, execution time, maintenance cost, and debugging experience. Avoid broad end-to-end coverage until the team has proven stable locators, deterministic test data, repeatable device provisioning, and clear ownership for flaky tests.

name: Helmfile
description:
Helmfile defines a declarative YAML specification to deploy and manage multiple Helm charts consistently across environments. It is one of the popular ways to orchestrate multiple Helm charts when deploying cloud-native applications, providing a more structured approach to managing complex deployments. Helmfile simplifies management of multiple Helm charts across different environments, enables better version control and reproducibility of deployments, and reduces complexity when managing microservices architectures.

The tool integrates well with GitOps workflows such as ArgoCD and Flux for automated deployments, making it ideal for complex applications with multiple services requiring environment-specific configuration management. However, for simple projects with only one Helm chart or basic deployments, Helmfile adds unnecessary complexity and standard Helm commands are sufficient. Teams should be aware that Helmfile introduces an additional layer of abstraction over Helm, requiring understanding of both concepts, and debugging can be more complex due to this additional layer.

name: K6
description:
K6 represents a modern approach to performance testing, built around a developer-centric philosophy and JavaScript-based scripting. The tool treats performance testing as code, enabling version control of test scripts, seamless CI/CD integration, and maintenance alongside application code. Its cloud-native architecture includes built-in support for modern protocols like HTTP/2, WebSockets, and gRPC, making it particularly well-suited for testing microservices and API endpoints.

K6 provides real-time metrics and threshold-based assertions that deliver immediate feedback during test execution. The tool's extensible architecture supports custom metrics and integrates with monitoring tools like Grafana and InfluxDB. Its lightweight footprint and container-friendly design make it ideal for distributed testing scenarios and cloud-native environments.

The tool's popularity stems from its ability to address the limitations of traditional performance testing tools like JMeter, particularly in environments where teams prefer code-based approaches over GUI-driven test creation. While K6 shows significant promise and addresses real pain points in performance testing, it's still new compared to established tools, and its JavaScript dependency and learning curve may present challenges for teams with limited frontend expertise. Organizations should assess K6's fit for their specific testing needs and team capabilities before committing to adoption.

name: Report Portal
description:
ReportPortal is an open-source, AI-assisted test reporting platform that aggregates results from across our automation stack — Playwright, Cypress, JUnit, K6 and dozens of others through native agents — into a single, navigable history with dashboards, trend analysis and root-cause categorization. The tool ingests test runs in real time, groups failures by signature so flaky tests stop drowning out real regressions, and uses ML-based auto-analysis to suggest whether a failed test is a known defect, a product bug or an automation issue. Self-hosted on Kubernetes, it integrates with Jira, GitHub, GitLab and our CI systems so a failed test is one click away from the offending change and the ticket that owns it.

We are placing ReportPortal in assess alongside the broader Test Reporting evaluation as a strong candidate for the shared, durable view of quality that our Test management tools and CI dashboards do not give us today. What to validate is ingestion volume and retention cost at our actual run rates, the quality of auto-analysis on our test patterns once it has been trained on our history, integration with the launch frameworks each portfolio team uses, and operational fit on our internal Kubernetes — including authentication via our existing identity provider and storage sizing for screenshots, traces and videos. Teams piloting it should optimize for shared dashboards across releases and a low-friction path from "this test failed" to "this is the change to look at", rather than for short-term per-team reporting wins.

name: Test Reporting
description:
As automated test suites grow across unit, integration, end-to-end and performance layers, raw CI logs stop being a useful artifact for anyone outside the team that wrote the test. Dedicated test reporting tools — for example Allure Report, Report Portal or vendor dashboards built into Azure DevOps and GitLab — turn run output into a navigable, historical view: pass/fail trends, flakiness hotspots, slowest tests, ownership and links from a failure straight back to the offending commit or test artefact.

We're placing test reporting in assess while we evaluate which combination of tools fits the way ASEE and Payten teams actually deliver software. The interesting questions are less about which UI looks nicer and more about: how reporting integrates with our Test management tools, how it surfaces signal during Factory acceptance testing, and how cleanly it plugs into the same pipelines that already host our quality gates and Feedback Loops for Agents. Teams piloting a tool should optimise for shared dashboards, durable history across releases, and a low-friction path from "this test failed" to "this is the change to look at".

name: Azure DevOps
description:
Azure DevOps is a comprehensive DevOps platform providing integrated services for version control, work tracking, continuous integration, and deployment. Its suite includes Azure Repos for Git version control, Azure Boards for agile planning and work tracking, Azure Pipelines for CI/CD, and Azure Artifacts for package management, all deeply integrated with the Microsoft cloud ecosystem.

While Azure DevOps offers mature capabilities and enterprise-grade security, our experience has revealed persistent challenges. The platform suffers from limited customization, complex licensing, and sub-optimal integration with non-Microsoft tools. Vendor lock-in creates dependency risks, and its user interface and workflows often feel dated compared to more modern, open alternatives like GitHub and Jira. Although Microsoft has modernized parts of the product—introducing YAML-based pipelines and improved GitHub integration—these changes have not fully addressed usability and ecosystem concerns.

Teams heavily invested in Azure DevOps may continue using it for stable workloads but should plan gradual migration toward more flexible, ecosystem-agnostic solutions that enhance developer experience and agility.

name: Docker Desktop
description:
Docker Desktop once served as the de facto way to manage local container environments on Windows, macOS, and Linux. It bundled Docker Engine, CLI, BuildKit, Compose, and an intuitive GUI that simplified networking, file sharing, and local Kubernetes. However, with the shift to a commercial licensing model for business use, it no longer fits most enterprise setups where multiple developers or teams use shared tooling.

The tool remains valuable for individual developers and small proof-of-concept work but introduces cost, compliance, and parity issues in regulated or large-scale environments. Alternatives such as Rancher Desktop, Podman Desktop, Minikube, kind, or Colima offer free, open options that align better with production parity and cost control.

Teams should hold Docker Desktop for new adoption and favor standardized setups using Docker Engine or Podman directly, ensuring licensing clarity and consistent developer experience across environments.
